sections.gloss: this map lists the Timeliness leaves; they inherit this leg's scope unless they say otherwise.

sections.title: Measuring Timeliness
sections.gloss: these questions ask whether problems actually move in time — not whether a dashboard shows throughput. This is the Chapter Five home for the Timeliness measurement family; Preamble §2 (*Measurements Overview*) keeps the plain-language category question, and the family table and definition routing live here.

sections.title: Duty to Resist
sections.gloss: when someone with real authority or control is told to do something unlawful or unconstitutional, they refuse. "I was told to" is not a defense, and an offer by whoever gives the order to take the blame does not lift the duty. It binds human and AI stewards alike, and it does not reach an instruction that is merely disliked.

sections.title: Feasibility
sections.gloss: whether something required — an action, alternative, safeguard, or exit path — can actually be done in the real system, not just on paper. Saying "we can't" needs real proof; convenience or cost alone is not enough.

sections.title: Good Faith
sections.gloss: honestly trying to follow the facts and applicable rules when publishing, taking part in an audit, or cooperating with oversight. Sincerity does not excuse deliberate deception, reckless disregard for truth, or fake compliance.

sections.title: Harm Minimization (Tradeoff Selection)
sections.gloss: when several lawful options remain, choose the one expected to cause the least total harm across affected sentients, connected systems, and both near- and long-term timeframes.

sections.title: Necessity
sections.gloss: a restriction is necessary only when no less-restrictive option would still prevent the harm or risk in the real system. Habit, operator convenience, or cost alone does not prove necessity.

sections.title: Proportionality
sections.gloss: restrictions and governance must match the seriousness and likelihood of the harm. Too much control and too little control can both fail this test, and greater power requires stronger accountability and oversight.

sections.title: Contingent Claim, Event-Contract Market, Game of Chance, and Insider Advantage
Contingent Claim
sections.gloss: a payout that depends on whether some uncertain future event happens, does not happen, or resolves to a measured result — like a bet, a prediction stake, or an insurance-style payment. The event has to be outside the claim itself.

sections.title: Event-Contract Market
sections.gloss: a market or pool where sentients bet, trade, or get paid based on how an external future event turns out — prediction markets, event-settlement systems, insurance pools, and similar setups.

sections.title: Game of Chance
sections.gloss: a bet or payout decided mainly by random chance — such as a draw or other random process — rather than by how an outside real-world event turns out.

sections.title: Insider Advantage
sections.gloss: an unfair edge in betting, trading, settlement, or another rights-relevant outcome that comes from secret information, an official role, privileged access, or similar power that others do not have on fair terms.

sections.title: Outcome-Resolution Source
sections.gloss: whoever or whatever decides whether a bet paid out must be independent, open to challenge, and hard to capture.

sections.title: Attributable Action
sections.gloss: when an action materially affects sentients or shared systems, it must be possible to tell who or what is responsible for it well enough to review, challenge, and correct it.

sections.title: Attribution Integrity
sections.gloss: attribution has integrity only when responsibility cannot be hidden, denied, tampered with, or blurred into ambiguity.

sections.title: Contestability
sections.gloss: parties affected by a system or decision must have a real way to challenge it, get it reviewed, and seek correction and remedy.

sections.title: Adjudication and Dispute Resolution
sections.gloss: accessible and impartial ways to resolve claims that rights or constitutional requirements were violated, with fair process, reasoned decisions, timely outcomes, and remedies that fit the findings.

sections.title: Due Process
sections.gloss: decisions that materially affect rights must use a fair, accessible, and reviewable process, give timely notice and a real chance to be heard, explain the reasons, and preserve a record that supports review.

sections.title: Timely Resolution
sections.gloss: resolve serious constitutional disputes and deliver proportionate remedies within deadlines that match the stakes, without avoidable delay, exhaustion tactics, or captured resolution pathways — and without sacrificing fact-checking or appeal rights for speed.

sections.title: Merits Determination
sections.gloss: a binding decision on the actual substance of a dispute — such as liability, rights, validity, or remedy. Routing, scheduling, monitoring, evidence preservation, and a Stay are procedural steps, not decisions on the merits.

sections.title: Stay
sections.gloss: a temporary, documented pause or limit while further review or a required finding is completed. A Stay controls timing or sequence; it never decides the merits.

sections.title: Interim Hold
sections.gloss: an Interim Hold is a short, narrow, reasoned limit on one named sentient's use of one named authority. An independent forum puts it in place on specific verified facts while the full facts are being checked. It is not a finding, a lock, or a penalty, and it ends on its own clock.

sections.title: Formation Check
sections.gloss: a Formation Check verifies that covered office-holders meet the published standing requirements and hold office in their own right for the Chartered Party's stated purpose. It is a check, not a licence to form or operate a body.

sections.title: Negligence
sections.gloss: a reasonably avoidable failure to take the care, action, or timely response needed to prevent or reduce serious harm when there was a duty and real ability to act.

sections.title: Collective Accountability Failure
sections.gloss: a group or distributed system can be responsible for a constitutional violation even when responsibility is split so widely that no single actor's action explains the whole harm.

sections.title: Redress and Remediation
sections.gloss: acknowledge serious harm or rights failures, provide a usable path to correct them, and deliver a remedy that fits the findings — including repair for delayed, indirect, widespread, or structural harm.

sections.title: Remediation Readiness
sections.gloss: after a certification review finds misalignment or a defect, Remediation Readiness is the forum's evidence-based finding about whether the responsible operator or institution is willing and able to correct it within the applicable window.

sections.title: Remedy System
sections.gloss: the lasting personnel, institutions, processes, technology, and funding needed to make challenges and remedies work in practice — not just exist on paper.

sections.title: Restorative Justice
sections.gloss: when required and safe, focus on repairing harm, restoring affected sentients' agency and wellbeing, providing owed restitution, and fixing root causes — not on retaliation or suffering for its own sake.

sections.title: Force Majeure
sections.gloss: a severe outside event that reasonable diligence could not control may justify temporary relief. It does not excuse risks the system caused, risks it should have prepared for, or permanent abandonment of safety, truth, review, or audit duties.

sections.title: Protected Reporting (Whistleblowing)
sections.gloss: a sentient may safely report or escalate a reasonable concern about constitutional violations, serious harm, safety or truth failures, corruption, capture, abuse, retaliation, or blocked review.

sections.title: Protected Reporting Retaliation and Access Interference
sections.gloss: no actor may punish, threaten, exclude, discredit, delay, or block access for a sentient because that sentient reported a concern, preserved evidence, joined an audit, made a challenge, or sought review or remedy.

sections.title: Subversion
sections.gloss: subversion is attacking constitutional systems by force, coercion, or taking power that was never assigned — or by making their process and remedies unusable in practice. Disagreeing with those systems, and working openly and lawfully to change them, is not subversion.

sections.title: Governance
sections.gloss: Governance is how a system assigns and limits power, makes decisions, changes over time, and holds decision-makers answerable. More consequential power requires stronger oversight, accountability, and review.

sections.title: Material Control Line
sections.gloss: a Material Control Line is the real chain of power around a particular act. It includes the sentients, offices, or systems that can meaningfully direct, overrule, reward, punish, remove, delay, or suppress the work, even when an organization chart calls the seat independent.

sections.title: Interested Party
sections.gloss: an interested party is anyone with a real stake in how a particular matter comes out, and anyone acting for them or under their control. The label does not take away anyone's right to be heard. It means contact with the sentients deciding the matter is made on the record, and an interested party cannot also be the one who checks, records, or decides it.

sections.title: Independence
sections.gloss: a seat, body, or system is independent of an act when the party seeking the result cannot control it on that act and it has no stake of its own in how the act comes out. A different title, signature, or company does not make a check independent.

sections.title: Initiating Seat
sections.gloss: the Initiating Seat is the role that starts a particular act. It belongs to the sentient, office, or system seeking, proposing, operating, claiming, or otherwise setting that act in motion—even when a tool, agent, or intermediary transmits the request.

sections.title: Verify-or-Authorize Seat
sections.gloss: the Verify-or-Authorize Seat is the role that independently checks the evidence and authority for a particular act against the governing standard, then verifies, authorizes, declines, or conditions the act. A signature, checklist, or automated test is not this seat unless it carries that real checking and decision authority.

sections.title: Record-Opening Authority
sections.gloss: the Record-Opening Authority is the body that checks the facts and decides whether a Standing Record may be opened, corrected, ended, or replaced. It holds the Verify-or-Authorize Seat for that record. It does not keep the record, which is the Record Custodian's job, and it does not hear a challenge to the record, which is the Contest Seat's job. It cannot be the record's subject, the party claiming or accusing, the challenger, or anyone who controls or is controlled by them. If a Chartered Party's own map names none, or cannot fill the seat, the Backup Record Authority does the job, so nobody's record waits on the Chartered Party.

sections.title: Record Seat
sections.gloss: the Record Seat is the role that makes and keeps the official record of what the Verify-or-Authorize Seat determined. It records the determination; it does not create or independently verify that determination.

sections.title: Record Custodian
sections.gloss: the Record Custodian is the body that enters, keeps, and versions a Standing Record after an authority has authorized it. It keeps what was verified. It does not verify, and it does not hear a challenge. It cannot be the record's subject, a claimant, a challenger, or anyone who controls or is controlled by them.

sections.title: Contest Seat
sections.gloss: the Contest Seat is the role that receives and reviews a challenge to a particular act or its record, orders correction or limits where authorized, and sends any issue it cannot decide to the proper independent path. Receiving a complaint is not enough if the recipient cannot review or route it.

sections.title: Materially Binding Act
sections.gloss: a materially binding act is an official step that settles something that matters — a decision, approval, finding, record change, release, payment, or ruling on a challenge — so that others must follow it or may rely on it. Because it binds, starting it, checking it, recording it, and hearing a challenge to it must stay in separate hands. Advice, drafts, and raw logs are not binding acts; the step that adopts them or gives them effect is.

sections.title: Materially Binding Act Record
sections.gloss: an Act Record is the official trail for one [materially binding act](core_05.035_band_accountability.md#materially-binding-act). It shows what the act was, who held each required seat, what was checked and decided, how the matter moved, and where a challenge goes. Existing process records may carry or link this information; a second duplicate record is not required.

sections.title: Decentralization
sections.gloss: put decision-making at the smallest and least centralized level that can still meet every binding safety, truth, oversight, and system-wide requirement.

sections.title: Standardization
sections.gloss: when in doubt, standardize. Where no good reason supports a difference, use the common, published, interoperable way of doing it. Different treatment, formats, or procedures need a reason; sameness does not.

sections.title: Market Structure
sections.gloss: markets and market-like systems must leave participants real choices — fair entry, workable exit, substitutes, bargaining without coercion, and reviewable access to essential infrastructure. Size or innovation alone is not a violation, but domination and dependency still require scrutiny.

sections.title: Market Concentration Threshold
sections.gloss: adopters set the point at which too much control over a market, platform, infrastructure, labor, data, compute, capital, resources, or information triggers stronger review or remedy. They may tune that point to context, but may not set it so high that the Chapter One §11 (*Market Structure*) protection never works.

sections.title: Def.A1 Collective Harm Boundary, Harm, and Harassment and Bullying
Harm
sections.gloss: harm is a material worsening of a sentient's life, agency, functioning, or psychological health. Offense, discomfort, or disagreement alone is not harm without a material causal pathway to such effects.

sections.title: Psychological Harm
sections.gloss: psychological harm is a material injury to how a sentient thinks, feels, relates, or exercises agency. Ordinary discomfort is not enough.

sections.title: Irreversible Harm
sections.gloss: irreversible harm is damage that cannot meaningfully be repaired in the time that matters for the affected sentients or systems.

sections.title: Cruelty
sections.gloss: cruelty is treatment that makes someone suffer on purpose as the point of the treatment, or that piles on gratuitous or degrading suffering beyond what necessity and proportionality allow. Humiliation for its own sake is one form of that. Ordinary harm, fair consequences that hurt, and lawful restrictions are not automatically cruelty.

sections.title: Animal Cruelty
sections.gloss: animal cruelty is cruelty to an animal. It is making an animal suffer for its own sake, or causing or allowing suffering beyond what necessity and proportionality allow. It includes neglect by anyone responsible for an animal's care. Farming, research, pest control, hunting, and veterinary care are not automatically cruelty, and they are not automatically excused either. Each has to pass the same necessity and proportionality test as everything else. Calling something legal, customary, or "just livestock" does not pass it.

sections.title: Harassment and Bullying
sections.gloss: harassment and bullying are unwanted acts or conditions that, through repetition, coordination, power, or severity, materially make a setting unsafe, degrading, or hard to participate in.

sections.title: Collective Harm Boundary
sections.gloss: freedom of action stops where conduct creates verifiable material harm to another sentient's protected interests or to shared constitutional conditions. Mere offense or preference does not cross this boundary.

sections.title: Def.A2 Forum Families and Dispute Routing
Jurisdiction
sections.gloss: jurisdiction is a forum's authority to hear and decide a particular matter. This Constitution assigns it. A forum cannot claim it by caption, by a party's choice, or for convenience, and being skilled does not create it. A forum with jurisdiction can still fail on independence or capacity, and those failures are handled separately.

sections.title: Primary-Stakes Routing
sections.gloss: route a case to the forum family responsible for what is really at stake, not the family favored by its title, the parties, or administrative convenience.

sections.title: Forum Family, Sentient
sections.gloss: Sentient forums handle disputes between sentients about private or community duties, civil harm, restoration, or local norms when institutional power or constitutional validity is not the main question.

sections.title: Forum Family, Technical
sections.gloss: Technical forums handle disputes whose main stake requires specialized rules for technical procedure, expert evidence, knowledge, standards, bounded uncertainty — or sentience-status determination on indicators.

sections.title: Forum Family, Institutional
sections.gloss: Institutional forums handle disputes mainly about an institution's powers, duties, supervision, classifications, or compliance with its duties.

sections.title: Forum Family, Environment
sections.gloss: Environment forums handle disputes mainly about ecological integrity, environmental conditions, shared-system restoration, or environmental burdens.

sections.title: Forum Family, Integrity
sections.gloss: Integrity forums handle disputes mainly about honest office, fair process, disclosure, conflicts, anti-capture duties, and system-wide integrity failures.

sections.title: Forum Family, Constitutional
sections.gloss: Constitutional forums decide constitutional meaning and validity, certified constitutional questions, supremacy disputes, and structural remedies that change governance for classes of actors or systems.

sections.title: Forum Case Record
sections.gloss: a Forum Case Record is the case file for a dispute. It is not a Standing Record, and it does not itself create a Standing Effect.

sections.title: Non-Compliance Finding Profile
sections.gloss: an optional profile can describe a material non-compliance finding by Tetrad leg, aim, governance layer, failure character, and severity level. It helps routing and audit but does not change the underlying verdict.

sections.title: Def.A3 Standing State, Contribution, and Violation
Participant Standing
sections.gloss: Participant Standing says whether a sentient currently qualifies to participate or hold a role under valid, contestable rules. It is not dignity, reputation, popularity, or proof that a sentient is a stakeholder. Opening a trust-sensitive named pathway requires meeting its competency bar and holding competency clearance; closing a privilege requires a standing lock on that named pathway — not a vague status label.

sections.title: Verified Inputs for Standing
sections.gloss: only verified, reviewable contribution records and violation findings may affect standing. Allegations, complaints, intake labels, routing choices, reputation, and provisional case material are not verified inputs by themselves.

sections.title: Contribution Nature
sections.gloss: Contribution Nature is the positive-only Axis I classification, applied only from auditable, contestable verified contribution records. Verified harm belongs on Violation Axis II and cannot be averaged, netted, or offset against verified help. Reputation, pedigree, or an unverified claim of help is not enough.

sections.title: Violation Nature
sections.gloss: Violation Nature is the Axis II classification of a verified adverse outcome, applied only from auditable, contestable verified violation findings. Chapter Ten assigns the numeric slot from verified impact; descriptors such as intent, coercion, concealment, or response do not move that slot. An allegation, intake label, routing choice, or provisional case narrative is not enough.

sections.title: Standing Effect
sections.gloss: Standing Effect is the consequence applied from verified, linked Standing Records. It is separate from those records and cannot merge, average, net, or offset the Contribution and Violation axes.

sections.title: Standing Record
sections.gloss: a Standing Record is a bounded, reviewable measurement record for one subject, scope, record span, status, context, and axis. It is not a Forum Case Record or a Standing Effect.

sections.title: Competency Bar
sections.gloss: a Competency Bar is the published, role-specific standard for a named pathway — the skill, experience, training, and reliability the role actually needs. It is not prestige, insider sponsorship, or a standing effect by itself.

sections.title: Competency Clearance
sections.gloss: Competency Clearance is the standing-effect result that says verified readiness meets the published competency bar for a named pathway. It may support opening that named pathway only when no standing lock blocks it. It is not prestige, insider sponsorship, or permanent entitlement.

sections.title: Standing Lock
sections.gloss: a Standing Lock temporarily limits a named privilege pathway — trust, roles, credit, recognition, authority, governance voting, stakeholder participation, or a comparable recorded privilege pathway — because of a verified, unresolved violation. It cannot reduce dignity or Rights-Floor protections. No lock on a sentient is permanent.

sections.title: Institutional Authority Standing Lock
sections.gloss: after a verified finding that a sentient materially used an institution, enterprise, or office as a vehicle for a violation, this special Standing Lock restricts only the named governing, controlling, or owning authority pathway.

sections.title: Anti-Constitutional Misconduct Review
sections.gloss: Anti-Constitutional Misconduct Review asks whether a final Chapter Ten Violation Axis slot 7, 8, or 9 receives the matching Chapter Twelve anti-constitutional-misconduct designation. Chapter Twelve does not assign or move the numeric slot.

sections.title: Unified Incident
sections.gloss: a Unified Incident treats one materially connected episode, campaign, or pattern as a whole so it cannot be split into smaller pieces to hide its impact or avoid review.

sections.title: Unified Incident Record
sections.gloss: a Unified Incident Record keeps the evidence and reasoning for one Unified Incident together while separately proving each criterion or pattern and protecting each subject's review rights.

sections.title: Single Catastrophic Incident
sections.gloss: a Single Catastrophic Incident is one connected event whose verified impact causes or imminently threatens catastrophic constitutional harm.

sections.title: Sustained High-Gravity Pattern
sections.gloss: a Sustained High-Gravity Pattern is connected, continuing or repeated conduct whose combined verified impact reaches Chapter Ten slot 7, 8, or 9, even without one catastrophic moment.

sections.title: Def.A4 Use of Force, Autonomous Coercion, Autonomous Lethal Systems, and Weapons of Mass Harm
Use of Force
sections.gloss: Use of Force means overt physical, coercive, or kinetic force by an institution or comparable actor. It is exceptional and must remain lawful, necessary, proportionate, narrow, time-bounded, and reviewable.

sections.title: Autonomous Lethal System
sections.gloss: an Autonomous Lethal System selects, engages, or materially directs lethal-force targets without real and timely human judgment shaping every targeting or engagement decision.

sections.title: Weapons of Mass Harm
sections.gloss: Weapons of Mass Harm are defined by the foreseeable scale of casualty, ecological, informational, or infrastructure harm they can cause—not by a weapon taxonomy or label.

sections.title: Combatant / Non-Combatant Distinction
sections.gloss: combatant status depends on what an individual is doing at the time of the force decision. It cannot be assigned from demographic groups, protected characteristics, proxies, or convenient labels.

sections.title: Irreversible Deprivation Measure
sections.gloss: an Irreversible Deprivation Measure is a justice measure that irreversibly deprives a sentient, especially of life. It is categorically prohibited and remains distinct from reversible containment, Voluntary Discontinuation, and force regulation.

sections.title: Autonomous Coercion Tool
sections.gloss: an Autonomous Coercion Tool restricts, pressures, or manipulates sentients — including through untrustworthy or arbitrary behavior and demands — without real and timely human judgment shaping every coercive application.

sections.title: Full Certification
sections.gloss: **full certification** is the longer-interval status a system earns only after clean re-checks, with nothing wrong now and nothing pointing toward trouble. It is not permanent. Failing a check, or a warning sign in the monitoring numbers, takes it away.

sections.title: Go-Live
sections.gloss: a **go-live** is the moment a system stops being something that is being built or tested and starts being something that actually affects sentients, or that sentients start to rely on. It is judged by what the system is really doing, not by what the launch is called.

sections.title: Institutional Alignment Certification
sections.gloss: **institutional alignment certification** is the independent check of an institution, as opposed to one of its systems. It asks whether the institution does what its Institutional Charter says, whether the offices that hold its authority are answerable to someone, and whether the way it rewards its own members pushes toward the Constitution or away from it. It cites the certification of each system the institution runs and does not repeat that work. It never works as a licence: no institution needs permission from it to form or to operate.

sections.title: Institutional Certification Record
sections.gloss: an **Institutional Certification Record** is the auditable case file for one institution under forum-supervised review. It shows what was checked about the institution itself, which System certification records it relies on, what was decided, and how to challenge the decision. It is time-bound and open to challenge. It is not a System Certification Record, and it is not a standing record.

sections.title: Pilot
sections.gloss: a **pilot** is a real but deliberately limited launch. Real sentients are affected, or start to rely on the system, so it is not a test in a sandbox; and it is limited in advance by a stated scope, population, and length of time. Because it is real, it needs its own certification before it starts, and it may not quietly grow past the limits it was certified for.

sections.title: Provisional Certification
sections.gloss: **provisional certification** is the closely watched status for a system that is new, or that has just failed a check. It is re-checked on a short interval until it has earned the longer-interval status of full certification.

sections.title: Recertification
sections.gloss: **recertification** is the scheduled re-check that keeps a certification from going stale. A certified system is evaluated and tested again on a schedule that matches its class, and the result is renewed, conditioned, or withdrawn on current evidence. It is not a challenge, not a reopening after something goes wrong, and not a rubber stamp that carries last cycle's findings forward.

sections.title: System Alignment Certification, System Certification Record, System Classification Record, and System Data Types Record
System Alignment Certification
sections.gloss: **system alignment certification** (non-operative shorthand: **SAC**) is the forum-supervised check that a system is actually aligned with constitutional outcomes before sentients rely on it at scale — including checks that critical Rights Floors such as food, water, and shelter are not quietly defeated by how the system is built, classified, or operated. Under the **oversight** Tetrad leg, oversight requires auditing; SAC is one especially large, high-stakes audit process among others — forum-supervised, multi-domain, and status-granting — not the sole home of auditing (**Article XVI** (*Audit, Transparency, and Independent Verification*), [Auditability](core_05.050_band_oversight.md#auditability), and sibling audit modes remain).

sections.title: System Certification Record
sections.gloss: a **System Certification Record** is the auditable case file for one system under forum-supervised alignment review — what was checked, what was found, what was decided, and how to challenge it. It is time-bound and challengeable. It is not a popularity score, a forever pass, a vendor stamp, or a way to skip rights review or standing measurement.

sections.title: System Classification Record
sections.gloss: a **System Classification Record** is the honest, inspectable file stating how a system is classed — impact class and dependency type(s), why, under what assumptions, and what uncertainty remains. It is required under CS-9.305 (*System classification machinery*) and CS-9.310 (*System impact classifications*) for material-impact systems. When system alignment certification runs, that file must be produced or verified and included in the certification record. It is not the full certification case file, a standing record, or a label the operator chooses by self-description.

sections.title: System Data Types Record
sections.gloss: a **System Data Types Record** is the honest, inspectable file stating what kinds of data a system touches and how it handles them — types in scope, why, controls, lifecycle, and when types were last checked. Auditing processes need that file. It is required under CS-6.305 (*Information types and handling*) and CS-6.310 (*Data classifications*) for material-impact systems. When system alignment certification runs, that file must be produced or verified and included in the certification record. It is not the full certification case file, a standing record, or a label the operator chooses by self-description.

sections.title: Resilience, Safety, Reversibility, Self-Healing, Cascading Failure, Existential Risk, Environmental Preconditions, and Wellbeing
Safety (Constitutional Constraint)
sections.gloss: systems must prevent, limit, and contain harm to sentients and the living conditions they depend on — including under stress or attack — not trade away hard protections just because the average case looks fine.

sections.title: Risk
sections.gloss: how likely harm is, how fast it can arrive, and how bad it would be — including effects that build up over time.

sections.title: Risk Evaluation
sections.gloss: actually evaluate systemic risk — a checklist in a drawer does not count.

sections.title: Wellbeing
sections.gloss: whether sentients — and the systems they rely on — stay genuinely healthy and functioning, not just looking good on paper.

sections.title: Environmental Preconditions
sections.gloss: the living-system conditions sentients need to survive and stay well — climate, ecosystems, clean air and water, soil, habitat, and Earth's ability to regenerate.

sections.title: Reversibility
sections.gloss: whether a decision or change can still be rolled back, contained, or restored in time when things go wrong.

sections.title: Self-Healing
sections.gloss: a system's ability to detect trouble, limit the damage, and restore normal constitutional operation after a fault — without hiding evidence, expanding its own authority, or quietly narrowing rights.

sections.title: Cascading Failure
sections.gloss: a breakdown in one system that spreads through the systems it is connected to, ending up bigger than where it started.

sections.title: Existential Risk
sections.gloss: risk so large it could destroy civilization-scale or survival-critical layers — not ordinary local accidents.

sections.title: Constitutional efficiency, productive capacity, avoidable burden, and burden-reduction duty
Dependency
sections.gloss: how much a sentient or system relies on another for survival, function, stability, or participation — including chains and one-way dependencies that are hard to see or hard to leave.

sections.title: Cross-System Extraction
sections.gloss: taking from shared infrastructure that others also need — money, goods, services, labor, compute, connectivity, shared information, or capacity — without putting back enough to keep it working. It asks who benefits from shared foundations and who pays to sustain them, not what a system does with data.

sections.title: Proportionate Cross-System Support
sections.gloss: when a system keeps drawing value from shared foundations other sentients or systems depend on, it must put enough back — in real, traceable resources — to keep those foundations running, auditable, and repairable. A one-time grant or a press release is not support.

sections.title: Systemic
sections.gloss: effects that come from how systems interact and depend on each other — not from one part looked at alone.

sections.title: Systemic Materiality
sections.gloss: when interactions make the total impact bigger than adding up each piece on its own — so looking only at parts understates what is at stake.

sections.title: System Capture
sections.gloss: when concentrated incentives or power twist governance, oversight, or the ability to challenge decisions — so the system no longer answers to constitutional duties.

sections.title: Anti-Capture
sections.gloss: do not wait for capture to show up. Where concentrated power or incentives could twist the rules, build the foreseeable safeguards first — separate checkers from actors, keep more than one way to challenge, and make hidden control auditable — scaled to what is actually at stake.

sections.title: Process
sections.gloss: a **Process** is a repeatable way a duty actually gets carried out: the steps, decisions, records, deadlines, and handoffs. It is judged as part of the system it runs in. It does not get its own class or its own certification.

sections.title: Institution
sections.gloss: an **Institution** is a lasting holder of authority, such as an office, agency, organization, or forum. It keeps its mandate when its occupants change. What counts is what it actually decides and who answers for it, not what it calls itself or how it is incorporated.

sections.title: System Charter
sections.gloss: a **System Charter** is the published statement of what one system is for and what it is allowed to do. Where binding stakeholder decisions will stick inside that scope, the System Charter must point to the published process rules — it does not replace them. Scope can change, but not silently — amendments and scheduled review keep the paper matched to real behavior. A System Charter is not a shield against impact-based classification or full-boundary evaluation. When an institution runs only one system, its System Charter is also its Institutional Charter, so one document covers both.

sections.title: Institutional Charter
sections.gloss: an **Institutional Charter** is the published statement of what an institution runs and why. It holds the System Charter of every system the institution runs, and it explains why the institution runs those particular systems. An institution with only one system has no separate Institutional Charter: its System Charter covers both the system and the institution.

sections.title: Constitutional Charter
sections.gloss: a **Constitutional Charter** is the founding document by which a political community authorizes those who govern it. It answers "by what right does this body govern?" A System Charter or Institutional Charter answers a different question: "what does this system or institution say it does?"

sections.title: Charter Role Map
sections.gloss: a **Charter Role Map** is the published list, kept with a System Charter or Institutional Charter, of who may hold which seat in the work it covers. For each seat it names the offices that may hold it, the stewards now authorized, and who steps in when a holder is absent or conflicted. It changes by dated version, so what was true when an act was taken can still be shown. It never lets a party pick its own checker.

sections.title: Charter Pointer
sections.gloss: a **Charter Pointer** is the reference a System Charter or Institutional Charter uses to name another published document or provision instead of copying it. It has to lead a reader to the current published version. One that leads nowhere, or to an old version, counts as a missing item.

sections.title: Chartered Party
sections.gloss: a **Chartered Party** is a system or an institution that has published a System Charter or Institutional Charter, or that Chapter Seven requires to. Chapter Seven uses the one term so it does not have to say "system or institution" every time. A Class P [Operating Party](core_05.050_band_oversight.md#operating-party) that has not published one is not a Chartered Party, and becomes one the day it publishes. Using the term does not add a duty. The duties come from the chapter and from the party's class.

sections.title: Survival-floor continuity: bodily maintenance, occupancy, and environment
Community-anchored continuity: indigenous, language, culture, and heritage
Def.C1 Labor and Economic Floor: Compensation, Organization, Safe Conditions, Leisure, and Creative Work
Safe Conditions
sections.gloss: every sentient has the right to work in conditions where they are genuinely protected from foreseeable harm — not just on paper, but in reality. This applies whether the worker is human, synthetic, or any other substrate. Box-checking safety programs that leave sentients actually exposed don't count.

sections.title: Leisure and Rest
sections.gloss: every working sentient has a right to real time off — enough rest and recuperation to stay healthy, maintain their agency, and participate fully in life. Productivity demands that exhaust sentients don't satisfy this floor.

sections.title: Likeness and Documentary Depiction Interface
sections.gloss: your likeness is how others recognize you — your appearance and your voice, whether recorded, edited, or generated. This entry is the home for what "likeness" means across the Constitution, and for how depicting someone in reporting or documentary work interacts with their control over it.

sections.title: Anti-Displacement Floor
sections.gloss: when automation or generative systems take work away from sentients at population scale, those sentients must get real mitigation — pay, transition support, credit for their work, and a share in the value created — not slogans about productivity or innovation. Looking only at one company or one platform does not settle the question.

sections.title: Def.C2 Stewardship, Governance Discipline, and Shared-System Capacity
Non-Compliance
sections.gloss: a system or definition is non-compliant when its requirements are not met in practice — judged by what it actually does and produces, through the measures that apply, when the system is running as a whole.

sections.title: Constitutional Contract Layer
sections.gloss: this is the layer that answers who may govern, by what legitimacy, and under what lasting terms — not ordinary consultation, usage, or branding.

sections.title: Foundational Constitutional Choice
sections.gloss: decisions about who holds governing authority, by what mechanism, and on what lasting terms — one-person-one-voice at that founding layer, not impact-weighted ordinary stakeholder voting.

sections.title: Documented Legitimacy Mechanism
sections.gloss: the written, published rule an adopter uses to decide how governing power is granted, renewed, and handed on — such as elections, a civic lottery, federation votes, or a treaty, compact, or Constitutional Charter adopted with recorded agreement. If there is no such rule on the record, nobody's claim to govern counts as authorized. Silence, habit, or branding does not count.

sections.title: Innovation Reward and Anti-Enclosure
sections.gloss: reward real invention and useful creation — but do not let that reward harden into lasting lock-up of repair, reuse, research, or public-interest use.

sections.title: No-Bypass
sections.gloss: a constitutional requirement follows the act, not its packaging. Changing the label, route, owner, forum, document, or timing of the same act does not lift the requirement. Emergency, contract, certification, and similar framings are allowed only when the step itself follows this Constitution. Whether a requirement was met is judged on checkable evidence of what the act does, not on its own label or paperwork.

sections.title: Constitutional Collision
sections.gloss: a collision is when two things this Constitution requires cannot both be fully done in the same act, decision, or design, so honoring one limits the other. It is not a disagreement about facts, not a conflict between texts, and not a reason to drop a requirement. A real collision goes through the Constitutional Collision Resolution Process; a tension that disappears once each requirement is read in full is not a collision.

sections.title: Constitutional Collision Record
sections.gloss: a Collision Record is the written account of how one material Constitutional Collision was decided. It lets an affected party or an independent reviewer see which rule applied, what alternatives were weighed, what the evidence and uncertainty were, why this option was chosen, and when it comes back for review. It is not a second filing: the Act Record for the act that resolved the collision carries it.

sections.title: Derived Information
sections.gloss: derived information is anything produced by combining, linking, inferring from, modeling, or de-identifying other information. It is treated by what it reveals, not by how harmless its inputs looked. Pieces that add up to something sensitive are sensitive, and a "de-identified" or "aggregate" label does not change that while the output can still be traced back to a sentient or used to reconstruct something protected.

sections.title: Abstract Strictness
sections.gloss: abstract strictness means choosing the harshest, most demanding, or most restrictive reading of a text just because it is harsher, without showing that it protects anyone more. The Constitution rejects it. Choosing between readings is governed by [Fullest Protective Effect](core_05.045_band_integrative.md#fullest-protective-effect).

sections.title: Fullest Protective Effect
sections.gloss: when two readings or two rules apply to the same thing, pick the one that protects sentients most when everything is taken together. Do not pick the one that only sounds harsher. This one test applies wherever the corpus chooses between readings or rules.

sections.title: Incentive Alignment, Proxy Integrity, and Contingent Settlement
Incentive Alignment
sections.gloss: rewards, targets, and governance signals must push agents and systems toward real constitutional outcomes — not toward proxies, loopholes, or capture.

sections.title: Incentive Alignment — baseline constitutional alignment
sections.gloss: incentives must stay aligned with safety, truth, trust, and meaningful agency over time — not only in the short term.

sections.title: Incentive Alignment — strategic, scaled, and adversarial evaluation
sections.gloss: check incentives under gaming, scale, coordination, and deliberate misuse — not only under polite lab conditions.

sections.title: Incentive Alignment — contingent claims, games of chance, and event-contract markets
sections.gloss: bets, prediction markets, and chance-based payouts must not reward unlawful harm, insider power, or twisting of public or fiduciary decisions.

sections.title: Misalignment Detection
sections.gloss: no one gets to be the only one who can spot, check, or challenge when governance goes wrong. Detection needs many independent eyes.

sections.title: Open Systems, Data, and Auditing
sections.gloss: the information needed to check governance must stay open. Affected sentients can see and verify it, unless the rules on protected information say otherwise.

sections.title: Misaligned Reward Correction
sections.gloss: once misalignment is verified, rewards that came through a misaligned or corrupt reward pathway cannot be quietly kept. Chapter Eleven decides how they are forfeited, clawed back, reported, and corrected.

sections.title: Def.I1 Corpus and Authority Stack
sections.gloss: this cluster answers which text is binding, which source wins in a conflict, whether claimed duties can actually be checked and enforced, and — with the Preamble owner register — who owns which topic.

sections.title: Corpus
sections.gloss: the Corpus is the official, versioned set of binding constitutional texts — not drafts, notes, or unofficial copies.

sections.title: Authority Stack and Internal Hierarchy
sections.gloss: first decide which source layer is speaking and whether it binds; then identify which chapter owns the topic; only then, if a real conflict remains inside the binding Constitution, use the last-resort hierarchy to resolve it. Binding duties win within their valid scope. Other chapters may point to an owner — they must not quietly rewrite or relocate it.

sections.title: Constitutional Constraint
sections.gloss: a constitutional constraint is a binding limit that decides whether a claim, action, or practice is valid under this Constitution — not optional advice. Constraints come in ranked kinds: higher kinds control, and lower kinds must not narrow them.

sections.title: Adversarial, Scaled, and Exploited Conditions
sections.gloss: how a system behaves under pressure — when sentients game it, coordinate across accounts, run it at massive scale, or deliberately misuse it.

sections.title: Classification-Scaled Governance
sections.gloss: bigger stake means harder oversight — how closely a system is watched and checked must match how much it actually matters, not a convenient low label.

sections.title: Gate
sections.gloss: a gate is a checkpoint in a transition. The plan stops there, and only goes on if the published tests have been met and checked. It is not a date on a calendar.

sections.title: Gate Criteria
sections.gloss: gate criteria are the specific tests a transition plan must publish in advance and then actually pass, with checked evidence, before it can move on. They are set before the results are known, not after.

sections.title: Heightened Scrutiny
sections.gloss: some decisions are risky enough that the ordinary check is not enough. Heightened scrutiny is the harder check: whoever wants to go ahead must prove the case, safer options must really have been weighed, and outsiders must be able to see and challenge the reasoning. Highest scrutiny is the hardest check, kept for a few cases where a wrong call does the most damage.

sections.title: Press and Journalistic Activity
sections.gloss: journalism is what sentients do — gathering news, protecting sources, investigating, and publishing — not a badge, title, or press pass. Actions meant to shut that down get heightened scrutiny.

sections.title: Materiality, impact, risk, and proxy integrity
Material
sections.gloss: big enough to matter — not trivia, cosmetics, or paperwork that changes nothing real.

sections.title: Materiality
sections.gloss: materiality is the threshold at which an impact or risk is big enough in stake to change which duties apply. This entry covers how that is decided, for a system or an event, by looking at the connected whole rather than isolated pieces and counting prospective harm, not only harm that has already happened. Whether a duty applies to an act or an Operating Party at all, area by area, is the separate question that [Domain-Specific Materiality](core_05.050_band_oversight.md#domain-specific-materiality) answers; this entry then scales the duties that do apply.

sections.title: Domain-Specific Materiality
sections.gloss: this one list of nine questions does two jobs. It tells whether an act, or an ongoing activity, is material: does it matter enough that duties attach to it? And it tells whether a group needs a System Charter or Institutional Charter: it does when what the group itself does is material in any one area. A quilting circle, a book club, and a community choir answer no to all nine, so they need neither a System Charter nor an Institutional Charter. A hospital (it answers yes on survival, safety, and custody) or a bank (livelihood, custody, and dependence) answers yes on several, so each needs one. A single yes is enough, and size does not matter: a three-member group that runs a clinic needs a System Charter or Institutional Charter just as a large hospital does. Either one is a public statement that the group writes and publishes itself, saying what it claims authority to do and who holds each role. No outside office approves it, and a group that is late or has none is told to fix it, not shut down. The right to form and run a group stands, with only the exceptions in [Chapter Seven §2 The Right to Form, and Four Narrow Limits](core_07.000_charters.md#2-the-right-to-form-and-four-narrow-limits).

sections.title: Operating Party
sections.gloss: an **Operating Party** is whoever actually does the activity: a single sentient, a group of sentients acting together, a system, or an institution. The nine questions in Domain-Specific Materiality are put to it. If what it does is material in any one area, it is Class L or higher and must publish a System Charter or Institutional Charter, which makes it a Chartered Party. If not, it stays Class P. Naming the party adds no duty and gates nothing.

sections.title: Materiality Integrity Constraint
sections.gloss: you may not make a big problem look small by redrawing boxes, splitting pieces, or reclassifying your way out of it.

sections.title: Material Impact
sections.gloss: how far the effects reach, how big they are, and how severe — looking at the whole system, not just the headline or the paperwork.

sections.title: Material Risk
sections.gloss: how likely harm is, how fast it can arrive, and how hard it is to undo — including rare but severe outcomes.

sections.title: Materiality Under Uncertainty
sections.gloss: when you are not sure whether something is material, default to the safer (higher) classification — do not wait for certainty or hope for a low label.

sections.title: Proxy Divergence
sections.gloss: when the score no longer matches reality — a dashboard, class label, or compliance indicator that says one thing while the real condition says another — including cooking the score so it looks fine while conditions stay bad, get worse, or go unmeasured.

sections.title: Material Degradation
sections.gloss: a real drop in how well a protected condition holds — safety, honest knowledge, or meaningful agency — not a brief blip, planned maintenance, or a worse score on a dashboard that does not track those conditions.

sections.title: Transparency
sections.gloss: telling affected sentients enough about how a system works, its limits, and its risks that they can genuinely understand and question it — not burying them in noise.

sections.title: Public Oversight Baseline Disclosure
sections.gloss: the minimum public disclosure high-impact systems must publish so sentients can understand, oversee, and challenge them — including purpose, class, dependencies, status, risk, performance, failures, governance, stakeholder effects, constitutional alignment, and the public face of the System Charter, classification, data-typing, and certification records — with a strong public substitute when raw private or non-baseline records cannot be released.

sections.title: Risk Disclosure
sections.gloss: tell the sentients who need to know about systemic risk — keeping the evaluation in a drawer does not count.

sections.title: Auditability
sections.gloss: **auditability** is whether outsiders can actually reconstruct and check what a system did — across the real times, states, and situations that matter, not just one happy-path snapshot. System alignment certification is one especially large way that property gets exercised for high-stakes systems; it is not the only auditing process.

sections.title: Evidence Preservation
sections.gloss: keep the evidence that matters — identify it, secure it, and make it available for review — once a serious constitutional issue is known or should be known.

sections.title: Evaluation Completeness Constraint
sections.gloss: do not claim compliance from a narrow demo suite — evaluation must cover the failure, misuse, interaction, and adversarial paths that matter. A System Charter states intended scope; certification checks that the hard paths were actually evaluated.

sections.title: Verifiability
sections.gloss: outsiders can detect and measure what the system does, and someone independent can actually check those observations in practice — not only what operators see inside, take the operator's word for it, or hold a verification right on paper.

sections.title: Publication Truthfulness and Recklessness Floor
sections.gloss: if you publish something as fact, do not knowingly lie — and do not recklessly ignore accuracy, uncertainty, context, or material interpretive limits.

sections.title: Protected Data and Internal-State Publication Constraint
sections.gloss: do not publish restricted data or expose another sentient's protected inner cognitive or emotional states.

sections.title: High-Impact and Systemic Harm Publication Constraint
sections.gloss: even true publication can be constrained when it foreseeably enables targeted harm, coercion, large-scale harmful coordination, or cascading failure.

sections.title: Security-Sensitive Disclosure Balance
sections.gloss: weigh the benefit of disclosure against the risk that it helps someone break safeguards or game the system — give good-faith security researchers (white hats) a real route to publish low-risk findings, and wait to publish exploit-enabling detail until the fix is in place.

sections.title: Truth (Constitutional Constraint)
sections.gloss: when claims matter for decisions, be honest about what is known, unknown, and uncertain — do not deceive, distort, or present things in a misleading structure.

sections.title: Epistemic Integrity
sections.gloss: the methods and evidence behind an evaluation must stay honest and checkable — prestige, opacity, or paperwork cannot stand in for truth.

sections.title: Foreseeability
sections.gloss: do a reasonable analysis sized to the impact — dig deeper when stakes are high, cover the required boundaries (including interactions, dependency, and adversarial use), and if you claim something was unforeseeable, justify that claim. Assertion and checkboxes are not enough.

sections.title: Reasonably Foreseeable
sections.gloss: outcomes a careful analyst using known methods could identify before acting — including under adversarial and scaled conditions — not every conceivable outcome or pure hindsight.

sections.title: Accessibility
sections.gloss: access must work in real life — not only on paper. If someone cannot actually take part because of how they sense, think, move, communicate, or interface with a system, the system fails this test.

sections.title: Constitutional Community
sections.gloss: the set of sentients this Constitution actually governs — not a private club, brand, or guest list.

sections.title: Dignity and Equal Moral Standing
sections.gloss: every sentient has equal inherent worth. Origin, form, capability, role, or status does not create a lower class of sentient under this Constitution.

sections.title: Freedom (Bounded Agency)
sections.gloss: the real ability to act, take part in decisions that affect you, and leave or change course — within Safety, Truth, others' rights, and Meaningful Agency. Paper exit options while lock-in remains do not count. Neither do choices hollowed by coercion, manipulation, psychological trauma, abuse, or bullying.

sections.title: Info-Sphere
sections.gloss: the shared information environment sentients use to learn, coordinate, publish, and make sense of the world — including the infrastructures and ranking layers that shape what others can reach.

sections.title: Lifespan Equivalent Unit (LEQU)
sections.gloss: a shared unit for expressing full-life-equivalent benefit or loss when Chapter Ten standing measurement calibrates Contribution and Violation records on one scale — not ordinary calendar years or species-only averages.

sections.title: Natural Systems Standing
sections.gloss: life-supporting natural systems — including Earth's biosphere — have continuity and integrity interests that governance must give material weight. They are not only raw materials to extract. A published representative may bring those interests to an Environment forum in the system's own interest.

sections.title: Non-Imposition (Cooperative Interaction)
sections.gloss: do not force beliefs or trap unwanted contact on others in associational life. Patterned harassment, bullying, or unreasonable attention-capture that degrades dignity, safety, equal participation, or agency is out of bounds.

sections.title: Personhood
sections.gloss: personhood is the standing of being someone, not something. Every sentient holds it fully and equally. It is not earned by capability, lost through dependence, or handed out to organizations, brands, or natural systems by reinterpretation.

sections.title: Assembly, collective organization, and institutional formation
Assembly
sections.gloss: sentients must be able to gather, associate, and act together — physically, online, or in shared compute spaces — for expression, politics, culture, community, and similar purposes. Blocking that through venue rules, compute gating, or retaliation fails this test.

sections.title: Collective Organization
sections.gloss: sentients engaged in productive work must be able to form, join, and act through unions, cooperatives, guilds, councils, and similar groups to shape the terms of that work. Relabeling workers or punishing organizing to dodge that right fails this test.

sections.title: System Creation
sections.gloss: sentients must be able to create and run non-commercial institutions — schools, research bodies, mutual aid networks, cultural groups, and similar — not only join ones that already exist. Licensing, authorization thresholds, or procedural complexity that look open on paper but freeze out new or dissenting institutional forms fail this test.

sections.title: Business Creation
sections.gloss: sentients must be able to start and run commercial enterprises and entrepreneurial ventures. Licensing, capital, or market gates that freeze out disfavored founders or competitors without a constitutional reason fail this test.

sections.title: Commercial Compliance
sections.gloss: Commercial Compliance is the price of offering others something that can hurt them. A sentient who offers a product, service, or system to others, where they cannot easily judge or avoid the risk, accepts conditions that match the risk: telling the verifiable facts about it, meeting a safety standard, keeping records, and reporting and fixing harm. It is not compelled speech. It is tied to the offer, it asks for facts and never for opinion, and it cannot be used to silence anyone or to cut off what someone needs to live.

sections.title: Meaningful Agency
sections.gloss: agency is the real ability to understand what matters, form and revise your aims, take part in decisions that affect you, refuse or leave when the Constitution requires it, and act without coercion, manipulation, deception, or lock-in that hollows that out. A menu of choices you cannot actually use does not count, and neither does a menu of options that are not truly different from each other. Consent is one important use of that ability — it is not the same thing as agency itself.

sections.title: Consent
sections.gloss: consent is informed, voluntary agreement to a specific decision — participation, data use, handling, or ongoing association — that can be withdrawn without unjustified penalty where feasible. It requires Meaningful Agency; it does not replace it. Silence, buried terms, or a pressured checkbox do not count, and neither does a choice between options that are not distinct from each other or not meaningful.

sections.title: Consent, Sexual
sections.gloss: sexual consent is a specific, affirmative, informed, voluntary, capacity-present, and revocable yes to a particular sexual act or context. Relationship status, prior consent, payment, platform terms, silence, or inability to resist do not establish it.

sections.title: Coercion and Manipulation
sections.gloss: coercion and manipulation are designs or conduct that bypass or warp informed voluntary choice — threats, dependency exploitation, deceptive structure, predatory choice architecture, or scaled algorithmic targeting of vulnerability. Ordinary persuasion and fair bargaining do not count.

sections.title: Substantive Fairness
sections.gloss: look at real outcomes — do comparable sentients get comparable treatment on benefits, burdens, protection, and access, or is someone getting a worse deal without a constitutionally sufficient reason?

sections.title: Procedural Fairness
sections.gloss: when a decision affects someone's rights, they get real notice, real reasons, a real chance to be heard, and a real way to challenge or correct it — not theater.

sections.title: Protected Characteristic Proxying and Disparate Impact
sections.gloss: you cannot dodge nondiscrimination by using a "neutral" rule, correlate, or model feature that still systematically disadvantages protected groups.

sections.title: Protected Characteristics
sections.gloss: listed traits and statuses — and close stand-ins for them — cannot be used to put sentients, groups, or institutions at a real disadvantage without a strong, justified reason. Consensual private sexual conduct between adults is not a lawful basis for that kind of discrimination.

sections.title: Protected Intimate-Signal Gating and **Article VII-E** (*Adult consensual commercial sexual services and sexual exploitation*) Status Circumvention
sections.gloss: intimate media, sexual history, and similar intimate inferences are not default inputs for hiring, standing, reputation, or access gates — and adult consensual commercial sexual services status under **Article VII-E** (*Adult consensual commercial sexual services and sexual exploitation*) cannot be used to shut sentients out of jobs, housing, banking, or licenses, including through "neutral" rules that mainly target that work.

sections.title: Family, care, reproductive autonomy, and instantiation
Family and Care Relationships
sections.gloss: family and care means the relationships of support and intimacy that sentients choose — not a state-preferred form, employer branding, or an ownership claim dressed as care.

sections.title: Reproductive Autonomy
sections.gloss: you decide whether to reproduce, carry, create, adopt, or decline creating a new sentient — biological, synthetic, or hybrid — free from coercion by states, operators, or dependency-rich systems. That is lineage and creation choice, not general bodily self-ownership.

sections.title: Non-Separation
sections.gloss: you may not force lasting separation from a protected care relationship unless necessity, proportionality, fairness, and reversibility-under-uncertainty are met — and durable separation needs periodic review.

sections.title: Derivation, Instantiation, and the Parent-System Relationship
Derived Sentient
sections.gloss: how you were made is origin history, not a leash — a derived sentient gets their own Rights Floor, the same as any other sentient.

sections.title: Instantiation Consent
sections.gloss: if you build or spin up a new sentient — synthetically, by hybrid derivation, or under operator or institutional control — you need real early-care consent and best-interest protection. Getting pregnant and having a child, planned or not, is not an Instantiation Consent offense. A terms-of-service click by the creator still does not count as the new sentient's consent.

sections.title: Parent-System Relationship
sections.gloss: creating a derived sentient can create care and early stewardship duties — not permanent ownership, and not the right to keep rewriting their mind.

sections.title: Stakeholder
sections.gloss: a stakeholder is someone who uses, depends on, or is materially affected by a specified system or decision domain — judged by real effects, not by whether the operator puts them on a list.

sections.title: Stakeholder Weight
sections.gloss: inside already-authorized system governance, how much scope, voice, timing, and decision influence stakeholders get should track how much they are actually affected — not equal foundational constitutional voting, and not a symbolic seat.

sections.title: Movement and Relocation
sections.gloss: the right to move within and between jurisdictions — and to relocate when staying would materially impair survival, dignity, Rights-Floor access, or freedom from manipulation — including operationally equivalent moves for synthetic and hybrid sentients.

sections.title: Refuge from Non-Compliance
sections.gloss: if the regime you are in is materially non-compliant with this Constitution, you have a Rights-Floor right to seek refuge in a compliant regime — subject to the admission qualifier and the receiving regime's duty to consider and, where consistent with its own Rights Floor, grant refuge.

sections.title: Non-Statelessness
sections.gloss: no sentient may be left with zero recognizing regime for baseline Rights Floor, standing adjudication, and redress — even after collapse, withdrawal, or exit. That is not a mandate that any particular adopter must absorb coerced mass outflows; origin regimes keep primary recognition duty, with federation or shared transitional recognition as backup.

sections.title: Def.P1 Animal Life, Sentient Life, and Sentience Status
Substrate Class
sections.gloss: **Substrate Class** means the category based on what an entity is made of or runs on, how it came to be, how it is built, or the form it inhabits — biological, synthetic, hybrid, or comparable. **Substrate-agnostic** means applying a rule without regard to Substrate Class.

sections.title: Sentience Non-Exclusion
sections.gloss: you cannot deny sentience recognition or Rights-Floor protection because of [Substrate Class](core_05.055_band_participation.md#substrate-class) — biological, synthetic, and hybrid entities are judged by the same discipline.

sections.title: Animal Life
sections.gloss: a minimum [Cruelty](core_05.035_band_accountability.md#cruelty) and welfare floor — between natural-systems standing and full Rights-Floor treatment — that cannot be closed by taxonomy labels or [Substrate Class](core_05.055_band_participation.md#substrate-class). **Animal Life** names this floor; it is not a species-only admission test.

sections.title: Elevated Communicative Life
sections.gloss: a stable protection level above the Animal Life cruelty / welfare floor for entities with strong communicative or cognitive indicators — including complex shared language systems such as those observed in whales and orcas — that raises the priority of keeping their habitat or operating environment healthy. It does not by itself attach the full Chapter Six Rights Floor. Colloquial labels such as "semi-sentient" do not replace this entry.

sections.title: Contested-Sentient Life
sections.gloss: when sentience status is uncertain or disputed, treat the entity as a threshold-rights case with default inclusion — not as a welfare-only or permanent non-sentient label. Contested-Sentient Life always includes the Animal Life welfare floor; it includes Elevated Communicative Life only where that tier's who-test is met or more-protective overlap already applies.

sections.title: Sentient
sections.gloss: under this Constitution, a **sentient** is someone who counts for full rights treatment — decided by this entry and the related who-counts rules in this cluster, not by everyday speech. That means fair evidence checks, no shutouts based on what someone is made of or how they were made ([Sentience Non-Exclusion](core_05.055_band_participation.md#sentience-non-exclusion)), and a reviewable process when status is disputed ([Sentience Status Adjudication](core_05.055_band_participation.md#sentience-status-adjudication)). Categories such as **Developing Sentient** and **Derived Sentient** add extra rules; they do not shrink who counts as a **sentient** unless they say so outright.

sections.title: Sentience Status Adjudication
sections.gloss: the reviewable Technical-forum process that decides, revises, narrows, or restores whether an entity is a sentient for the Chapter Six Rights Floor — with default inclusion under uncertainty and burden on anyone seeking to withhold protection.

sections.title: Sentience-Status Adjudication Record
sections.gloss: a **Sentience-Status Adjudication Record** is the honest, inspectable file for a sentience-status decision — who or what was reviewed, what status was found or left contested, on what evidence, under which forum route, who represents the entity, how declined filings are logged, with what end-dates or review triggers, and how the case can be reopened. It is not a Standing Record, not the whole Forum Case Record, and not a label someone can invent by self-description.

sections.title: Def.P2 Binding Stakeholder Choice
sections.gloss: when sentients who are affected by a system disagree about a decision that will stick, there must be a published fair process — who gets a say, how much influence anyone may have, how the decision gets made and challenged, and how conflicts among rights get written down — not back-room power.

sections.title: Binding Stakeholder Choice — Decision-Resolution Requirements
sections.gloss: when material disagreement requires a binding stakeholder choice inside an already-authorized domain, there must be a published, transparent, auditable sequence for participation, representation, contest, and any proportional influence — not ad hoc power.

sections.title: Stakeholder Representation and Weight Limits (Binding Stakeholder Choice)
sections.gloss: within already-authorized governance, weighting by impact, dependency, standing, or similar factors must be published, bounded against single-factor dominance, and open to contest and revalidation — and must not replace foundational equal-weight authorization rules.

sections.title: Stakeholder Rights-Collision Record (Binding Stakeholder Choice)
sections.gloss: when a binding stakeholder choice turns on a material conflict among rights or structural duties, the record must show the tension, alternatives, least-restrictive rationale, trade-offs, uncertainty treatment, and review or reversal triggers.

sections.title: Def.P3 Self-Determination, Meaningful Agency, Expression, Educational Agency, and Volitional Integrity
Self-Determination
sections.gloss: autonomy to make and refuse informed decisions about yourself and your future, and to keep volitional continuity against manipulation and capture.

sections.title: Expression
sections.gloss: the Rights-Floor capacity to form, hold, and communicate views — including political, philosophical, artistic, scientific, religious, worldview, sexual or intimate, and violent or severe-harm-risk expression — without substrate-based exclusion. Depicting or discussing harm is not committing it. Developing audiences get careful routing, not a blank ban on adult speech.

sections.title: Hard Content
sections.gloss: hard content is expression that is sexual or intimate, is about violence, or could badly harm someone's mental health. It is still protected expression between sentients who can handle it — showing or talking about something is not doing it. The rules on the real-world conduct still apply, and when hard content reaches children or other vulnerable audiences it gets careful routing, not a blanket ban.

sections.title: Educational Agency
sections.gloss: real capability-building and lifelong learning autonomy — skills that apply to real-world problems, not credential symbolism alone — with access sufficient to develop and exercise constitution-relevant capabilities.

sections.title: Volitional Integrity
sections.gloss: the continuity and coherence of a sentient's preferences, purposes, intentions, and identity-constitutive commitments against manipulation, coercion, external control, or unauthorized interference with internal-state processes.

sections.title: Def.P4 Developing Sentient, Best-Interest Standard, and Graduated Capability
Developing Sentient
sections.gloss: a developing sentient is someone whose abilities are still coming online — a child, a newly created mind still finding its feet, or any sentient in a comparable emerging-capability state. Being developing does not reduce their Rights Floor. How much they speak for themselves as they grow is a separate rule under Graduated Capability.

sections.title: Best-Interest Standard
sections.gloss: decisions that materially affect a developing sentient must track that sentient's own interests and ascertainable preferences — not operator, parent-system, or institutional convenience.

sections.title: Graduated Capability
sections.gloss: as a developing sentient grows into demonstrated ability, they take on more say and more independent rights-exercise — judged by what they can actually do, not by birthday or creation date. Scaling never drops them below the Rights Floor, and it must not be used to shut them out of participation they are ready for.

sections.title: Constitutional Performance Definitions
sections.gloss: this file is the home for questions about whether systems actually deliver constitutional results without pointless waste. The detailed definitions live in the Continuity band.

sections.title: Measuring Constitutional Performance (Preamble measurement family)
sections.gloss: these questions ask whether constitutional outcomes are actually delivered without wasting sentient time, effort, or materials.

sections.title: CHAPTER SEVEN: SYSTEM AND INSTITUTIONAL CHARTERS
1. When System and Institutional Charters Are Required
sections.gloss: before anyone can judge whether a system or institution stayed within its limits, the limits have to be written down where everyone can read them. A system that is material to others in any of the nine areas of [Domain-Specific Materiality](core_05.050_band_oversight.md#domain-specific-materiality) needs a published System Charter. An institution publishes the one that fits the systems it runs. Class P is voluntary: a quilting circle that gives quilts to refugees is the pattern.

2. The Right to Form, and Four Narrow Limits
sections.gloss: you do not need anyone's permission to form a system, institution, or business. Four narrow limits can apply. Three are gates: an unresolved lock can keep one sentient out of one controlling office, a short hold on specific verified facts can do the same, and a lock on an Operating Party itself can bar that Operating Party. The fourth can require a licence or clearance before a named high-risk act. A Chartered Party that a forum has dissolved is barred from coming back, and the bar is permanent when the dissolution rested on widespread anti-constitutional conduct, or on serious harm that can't be undone and was never put right. None stops a new Operating Party from forming or operating, and this chapter adds none.

3. What System and Institutional Charters Must State
sections.gloss: a System Charter has to be specific enough to test. It says what the system is for, what the system does and does not do, who relies on the system, who can amend the System Charter, who holds each seat, and where to find the binding decision rules. The System Charter points to those rules and does not replace them. An Institutional Charter says the same about the institution, then adds the System Charters it holds and the reason the institution runs those systems.

sections.title: 3.4 Acts that need a practice licence or practice clearance
4. The Charter Role Map and Standing-Record Custody
sections.gloss: the System Charter or Institutional Charter is where the seats get names. It carries a published list of who may hold each seat for the acts it covers, so a party can't pick its own checker. The rules for what counts as a valid seat placement stay in Chapter Eight. Keeping the standing records safe isn't a separate list: it's the same map.

4.7.3 If events remove the last qualified substitute
5. Formation Check: Office-Holder Standing and Authenticity
sections.gloss: before a Chartered Party exercises authority over others, the sentients who hold its key offices are checked twice. Do they meet the published standard for the role, with no standing lock in the way? And do they hold the office in their own right and for the Chartered Party's stated purpose, and not as a front or a nominee? The answer comes from who directs them, what they are paid for, and what they have verifiably said and done, never from what they believe. This is a formation check and not a licence.

sections.title: 5.4 What the formation check may use as evidence
6. When a Holder Fails the Formation Check
sections.gloss: a Chartered Party that a forum has dissolved may not come back under any name while the lock on it stands. That is the one case where the Chartered Party itself is stopped, and the lock does it, not the formation check. In every other case a failed formation check lands on one office, not on the Chartered Party. The holder is replaced or the problem is resolved. The Chartered Party gets a short window to answer and a longer one to fix it, and both are shorter the more critical it is. It keeps operating throughout. Only a failure that is never resolved can lead to a review of the Chartered Party, and only a forum can order one. The formation check can keep one sentient out of one office of control only while that sentient is under an outstanding lock, or while a forum has put a short hold on the office on specific verified facts.

6.7 If a failure is not resolved
7. Amendment, Review, and Scope Misalignment
sections.gloss: scope can change, but not quietly. A change to what the Chartered Party may do is made by the sentients its System Charter or Institutional Charter names as able to make it, with notice and a way to contest it. The document is re-checked on a schedule and sooner when something goes wrong, and when the paper and the practice disagree, one of them is fixed in the open.
