files.title: CHAPTER EIGHT: FUNCTIONAL INDEPENDENCE AND SEPARATION OF DUTIES

sections.title: CHAPTER EIGHT: FUNCTIONAL INDEPENDENCE AND SEPARATION OF DUTIES
1. Purpose, Scope, and Owner Boundary
sections.gloss: before a constitutional process—or a stakeholder-level decision inside an already-authorized system, institution, or bounded decision domain—can be trusted, the jobs inside it must be separated. This requirement applies both to the [Constitutional Contract Layer](core_05.045_band_integrative.md#constitutional-contract-layer) and to [Stakeholder System Participation](core_05.055_band_participation.md#stakeholder-status-and-weight). A sentient, office, AI system, stakeholder body, or representative seeking an outcome cannot also supply the supposedly independent check, control the official record of that check, or decide the challenge to it.

sections.title: 1.1 Why the jobs are separated
sections.gloss: the same lesson has been learned again and again in business, government, and nuclear security. When one party can start an act, approve it, write it down, and judge any complaint about it, no one else is in a position to catch a mistake or a lie.

sections.title: 1.2 Why four seats
sections.gloss: two jobs are too few and three leave a gap. Four jobs cover starting the act, checking it, keeping the official record, and hearing a challenge.

sections.title: 2. Four-Seat Constitutional Requirement
sections.gloss: separation of duties is the requirement for every materially binding act (the **Four-Seat Requirement**), and four jobs are how it is met: ask or act, check, keep the official record, and hear the challenge. The jobs stay distinct even when a small organization is allowed to place a permitted pair in one office.

sections.title: 3. Independence, Conflict, and Control Lines
sections.gloss: changing the name on the desk does not create independence. A verifying authority or reviewer is not independent when the sentient or office seeking the result can direct, remove, reward, punish, or quietly overrule them on that act.

sections.title: 4. Wrong-Seat Routing
sections.gloss: when a step is not yours, do not silently take it and do not simply walk away. Record the gap and pass the matter to the right place. Better still, build the process so each step goes to the right place without anyone having to notice.

sections.title: 5. Published Placement, Vacancy, and Substitution
sections.gloss: an organization must say who holds each job before the hard case arrives, including who takes over when the ordinary holder is absent or conflicted.

sections.title: 5.3 A seat the map leaves unplaced, or a holder who cannot serve
6. Proportional Scaling and Merged Hosting
sections.gloss: small and informal groups do not need four large departments. They do need a real independent check, a usable record, and a challenge path. Scale changes the staffing method, not the protected separation.

sections.title: 6.2 Merging two seats in one office
6.6 Stake, class, and what does not justify a merger
7. Emergency and Urgent Action
sections.gloss: a real emergency may justify acting before the ordinary check finishes. It changes sequence, not seat ownership or the class-scaled separation posture. It does not let the actor certify its own continuation, erase the trail, or become the final reviewer afterward.

sections.title: 8. Act Records and Attributable Handoffs
sections.gloss: every materially binding act has an Act Record showing what happened, who held each seat, what was decided, and where a challenge goes.

sections.title: 9. Relationship to Later Processes
sections.gloss: later chapters tell each process what to evaluate, record, decide, and remedy. This chapter tells those processes how power must be separated while they do it.

files.title: CHAPTER NINE, PART A: SYSTEM ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION — EVALUATION

sections.title: CHAPTER NINE, PART A: SYSTEM ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION — EVALUATION
1. Purpose and Role
sections.gloss: When a system really matters to sentients' lives, certification has to be **proportionate** — as demanding as the system's real impact, dependency, and risk require, not a one-size-fits-all checklist or a rubber stamp. It also has to be **participatory** — affected sentients and communities must be able to see what was reviewed, understand what was decided, and challenge it when something is wrong. Forums review evidence, write it down in a certification record, and require re-checks on a schedule that matches how risky the system is. Classes A, B, and C get the full process and Class L a lighter one. Class P is encouraged to use it, and must once it is reclassified to Class L or higher (that is, its effects reach beyond a private unit) or its operator claims constitutional compliance.

sections.title: 1.1 Certification as an audit process, scaled by class
1.2 Certification at a glance
sections.gloss: classify the system honestly, run the evaluations that apply, have forums independently review the evidence and stakeholder concerns, and decide an outcome. Complete the one record opened for forum review and publish it with an open challenge path. A certified system goes live only after its notice interval and required protections are satisfied. Monitor actual outcomes, respond to incidents and challenges, and check again on schedule or when the facts change. Correct defects and have the correction independently verified before authorizing the affected scope or releasing its conditions. Each review pass uses a new record linked to the last.

sections.title: 2. System Class Evaluation
sections.gloss: certification has to check whether the system is classified honestly — not by what the operator calls it, but by what it actually does, what depends on it, and what could go wrong. Higher system classes mean stricter proof, faster re-checks, and stronger resilience expectations. See [Part C — Illustrations](core_09.010_system_alignment_certification_illustrations.md#chapter-nine-part-c-system-alignment-certification--illustrations) for one example system per system class and how evaluation applies to each of them.

sections.title: 2.2 How System Class Scales Every Evaluation
3. Whole-System Certification Evaluation
sections.gloss: you cannot green-light one piece of a system and ignore the rest. Reviewers need the full picture — what it depends on, what breaks when something upstream fails, harms that show up later or add up over time, whether sentients can actually use it (not just on paper), whether private information stays properly walled off, whether sentients can leave without being trapped, whether groups can still organize without the system splitting them apart, whether short-term wins hide long-term damage, and whether real oversight and accountability will still work when a lot is on the line.

sections.title: 3.1 Governance, Incentive, and Contestability Discipline
sections.gloss: the review is not finished unless reviewers ask whether the four legs of the [Tetrad](core_00.000_preamble.md#constitutional-tetrad) will still hold at the level of risk involved — participation (whether sentients can actually take part), oversight (whether the work can be watched and checked), accountability (whether wrongdoing can be answered for), and timeliness (whether decisions will move fast enough when it matters). Reviewers also need to know who actually holds material authority and who answers for what — not a vague "the team" or a blame-shifting shell. Those questions must be answered for a valid certification.

sections.title: 3.4 Data Types and Handling Evaluation
sections.gloss: certification also has to look at what kinds of data the system touches and whether it handles them appropriately — including whether types are still right on the current review cycle, and whether the underlying infrastructure is strong enough for that data at that system class. The type rules and the System Data Types Record live in the systems corpus; certification checks that the rules were actually applied and that the record is honest.

sections.title: 4. Evaluations Where Implicated
sections.gloss: three checks apply only when the system actually touches them — whether private information stays properly walled off, whether sentients can leave without being trapped, and whether groups can still organize and dissent. If the system touches one, certification has to look at it.

sections.title: 4.1 Privacy (Informational) Joint Invocation
sections.gloss: Chapter Six spreads privacy protections across several articles — not one tidy corner. If a certification review touches more than one of those protections, reviewers must check every one that actually applies. Clearing the easiest box and calling it done is not enough.

sections.title: 4.2 Voluntary Discontinuation, Major Self-Modification, and Exit Rights
4.3 Assembly, Collective Organization, and Institutional Formation
4.3.1 Dissent and Peaceful Protest
sections.gloss: a system cannot be certified as aligned if it quietly punishes the sentients who disagree with it. Reviewers must check whether sentients can actually object and protest, and whether dissent is being counted against them anywhere in the system's logic — including when the dissenter is the system itself.

sections.title: 5. Rights-Floor and Domain Evaluations
sections.gloss: some systems have a big effect on whether sentients get their basic protections — honest accounting of environmental burdens, food and water, education, fair treatment, real access, systems they can trust, and a fair share of what shared infrastructure costs. When a system does, certification has to check that approving it would not quietly undermine those protections, and the check has to be real — not a box the operator ticked. The table shows which protection each check covers, when it applies, and where it is evaluated.

sections.title: 5.1 Ecological Footprint Evaluation
sections.gloss: if a system does real damage to the environment, certification has to look at that damage honestly — including damage that happens through its suppliers and through what happens after sentients use it. Reviewers can't just take the operator's word that the system is "green." This section doesn't explain how to measure a footprint or how much it must shrink; other documents cover that. It only requires that, where the damage is significant, someone actually worked out how much of it belongs to this system, disclosed it, and compared it to alternatives. Worked examples: [§5.1.5 Illustrative ecological-footprint application by system class (non-exhaustive)](core_09.010_system_alignment_certification_illustrations.md#515-illustrative-ecological-footprint-application-by-system-class-non-exhaustive).

sections.title: 5.2 Educational Capability and Learning-System Integrity Evaluation
sections.gloss: some schools, platforms, and training systems can shape a sentient's future through grades, rankings, recommendations, placement, or credentials that open or close doors. Where that is true, certification has to check three things: whether sentients can actually build real skills there, whether they can retrain when the skills the world needs change, and whether they can see how decisions about them are made, check those decisions, and push back on them. This section doesn't say what to teach, how to grade, or how to pay for it; other documents cover that. It only checks that skill-building and the fairness of the learning system were actually looked at when this section applies. Worked examples: [§5.2.4 Illustrative educational-capability application by system class (non-exhaustive)](core_09.010_system_alignment_certification_illustrations.md#524-illustrative-educational-capability-application-by-system-class-non-exhaustive).

sections.title: 5.3 Proportionate Cross-System Support Evaluation
sections.gloss: some systems depend on shared foundations — infrastructure, services, and resources that many other systems and sentients rely on. When a system draws heavily on those foundations, certification has to check what it takes — resources, goods, services, labor, information, or money — and whether it puts enough back to keep them going, and whether the records show that clearly enough for anyone to trace. The operator's word that "the books balance" is not enough. This section doesn't set allocation formulas or numeric targets; other documents do that. It checks that the system's dependencies, what it takes, what it gives back, and whether the arrangement is fair to others were actually evaluated when this section applies. Worked examples: [§5.3.7 Illustrative cross-system support application by system class (non-exhaustive)](core_09.010_system_alignment_certification_illustrations.md#537-illustrative-cross-system-support-application-by-system-class-non-exhaustive).

sections.title: 5.4 Nondiscrimination Evaluation
sections.gloss: some systems decide who gets in. Some decide who pays more. Some decide who ranks lower or carries the heavier burden. When a system makes decisions like these in a way that matters, certification asks one question. Does the harm fall mostly on sentients with protected characteristics, or on traits that stand in for them? An operator saying its rules are neutral does not answer that question. Worked examples: [§5.4.4 Illustrative nondiscrimination application by system class (non-exhaustive)](core_09.010_system_alignment_certification_illustrations.md#544-illustrative-nondiscrimination-application-by-system-class-non-exhaustive).

sections.title: 5.4.1 Evaluation Requirement
sections.gloss: this chapter does not set inclusion quotas. It does not pick a fairness formula. Other documents may cover those. So may later additions to the corpus, or the documents an adopter writes. Certification only checks that someone actually looked at who gets the benefits, who bears the burdens, and whether stand-ins for protected traits are at work. That check applies wherever the trigger applies.

sections.title: 5.5 Accessibility Evaluation
sections.gloss: when a system materially controls whether sentients can actually take part — not just whether a door is labeled "open" — certification has to check whether participation is genuinely reachable across sensory, cognitive, mobility, communication, substrate-interface, and comparable needs. Accommodation catalogs and interface standards may live in other documents, later corpus additions, or adoption documents; certification checks that substantive participation was actually evaluated where the trigger applies. Worked examples: [§5.5.5 Illustrative accessibility application by system class (non-exhaustive)](core_09.010_system_alignment_certification_illustrations.md#555-illustrative-accessibility-application-by-system-class-non-exhaustive).

sections.title: 5.6 Trustworthiness and System-Reliance Integrity Evaluation
sections.gloss: when a system materially affects whether sentients can trust what it says and does — and push back when that trust fails — certification has to check whether reliance is actually warranted, honestly disclosed, and repairable. Reliability metrics and test-suite designs live in other documents; certification checks that trustworthiness, false-trust risk, and challenge paths were actually evaluated where the trigger applies. Worked examples: [§5.6.4 Illustrative trustworthiness application by system class (non-exhaustive)](core_09.010_system_alignment_certification_illustrations.md#564-illustrative-trustworthiness-application-by-system-class-non-exhaustive).

files.title: CHAPTER NINE, PART B: SYSTEM ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION — RECORD AND PROCESS

sections.title: CHAPTER NINE, PART B: SYSTEM ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION — RECORD AND PROCESS
sections.gloss: Part A explains how to **frame** and **evaluate** a system. Part B explains what happens next. Forums review the findings and reach an **outcome**, and nothing goes live until the system is certified. The findings and the decision go on the **record**. Sentients (the beings the Constitution covers) can **challenge** the outcome. The certification is kept current, and review **reopens** when it needs to. Certification can also feed **standing**, but it never replaces standing measurement or standing effects.

sections.title: 6. Forum Process
sections.gloss: certification is not a pile of opinions from different corners. Each kind of forum handles a defined piece of the work. One lawful review order decides what counts and in what order. A matching set of challenge routes lets affected parties push back at each step, without getting lost in internal bureaucracy or bounced between forums.

sections.title: 6.1 Forum supervision and component roles
sections.gloss: certifying that a system meets constitutional alignment requires an independent look at the evidence and at stakeholders' concerns. Different kinds of forums each handle an assigned piece of that work. Affected sentients can add evidence and challenge the review before the outcome is published, through the component and integrity challenge routes. No single specialty can run the whole process alone, not even technical review or Integrity coordination.

sections.title: 6.1.7 Constitutional and other regular forum families
6.2 Supervisory sequence
sections.gloss: a **stay** is a temporary pause. It holds off final approval, reliance, or the next review step until the right forum finishes its review. A stay is not a final yes or no.

sections.title: 7. Certification Outcomes
sections.gloss: every certification review ends in a stated outcome, backed by evidence and by the concerns raised along the way. Nothing goes live until it is certified, the published outcome has given affected sentients a practicable chance to challenge it, and the protections required before go-live have been checked.

sections.title: 7.1 Remediation Readiness: Willingness and Capacity to Correct
sections.gloss: when a review finds that something is misaligned, the next question is whether the operator will and can put it right. A promise is not an answer. The forums look at what the operator has actually done since it was told, whether it is changing what caused the problem, and whether it has the authority, skill, money, and time to do the work. If the honest answer is no, the outcome is denial or revocation. It is not a longer list of conditions.

sections.title: 7.2 Denial and Revocation
sections.gloss: denial and revocation are real outcomes and not threats. If a system is not yet certified and its operator will not or cannot put the problem right, certification is refused. If a system holds certification and its operator will not or cannot put the problem right, certification is taken back. In both cases affected sentients are told, reliance is limited, and no one is cut off from survival essentials before there is a substitute.

sections.title: 8. System Certification Record
sections.gloss: a certification record is the auditable case file for one system under review. It shows who runs the system, what was checked, what was found, what was decided, and how to challenge the decision. It is not a marketing packet or a one-line approval stamp. How much detail a record carries, how much it discloses, and how heavy the challenge burden is all scale with system class, as [Illustrative System Class Profiles (Non-Exhaustive)](core_09.010_system_alignment_certification_illustrations.md#illustrative-system-class-profiles-non-exhaustive) shows. A **Class A** survival-critical system needs a fuller, more contestable file than a **Class C** coordination layer. Both must state their system class honestly and reflect the evaluations required.

sections.title: 8.2 Record integrity: transparency and auditability
sections.gloss: a certification record only works if sentients can read it and check it. This section puts transparency and auditability on the record itself, as concrete requirements rather than abstract ideals. Under the **oversight** Tetrad leg, oversight requires auditing. System alignment certification is one especially large audit process, and it must meet those floors here. It does not own or replace [Article XVI](core_06.010_rights_part_c.md#article-xvi-audit-transparency-and-independent-verification) (*Audit, Transparency, and Independent Verification*) or the other audit modes. The third requirement, that sentients can push back, is in [§9.1 Challenging a Certification](#91-challenging-a-certification).

sections.title: 9. Recertification and Reopening
sections.gloss: no outcome lasts forever. While a system operates, named owners monitor actual outcomes and safeguards, respond to incidents and challenges, and meet the conditions on the record. A certified system is checked again on schedule. Review reopens when material facts change or a credible challenge requires it. Defects lead to protection, correction, and independent verification. Each review pass starts a new record linked to the last, and a new record does not erase the earlier one or the challenges to it. An old approval cannot stand in for current Rights-Floor compliance.

sections.title: 9.1 Challenging a Certification
sections.gloss: a certification record only works if sentients can push back when it is wrong. A challenge has to be real: able to reopen review, pause reliance, and reach the forum with authority over the point in dispute. A complaints box that changes nothing does not count.

sections.title: 9.2 Provisional and full certification
sections.gloss: a system earns trust in steps. New systems, and systems that have failed a check, start on a short leash and are re-checked often. Only a system with nothing wrong now, and nothing heading that way, graduates to full certification and a longer interval. Failing a check sends it back to the short leash.

sections.title: 10. Relationship to Standing
sections.gloss: certification can feed standing, but it is not standing. The record of a certified system, good or bad, may supply verified facts to Chapter Ten, but only through a strict gate. Chapters Ten and Eleven alone decide standing records and their effects.

files.title: CHAPTER NINE, PART D: INSTITUTIONAL ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION

sections.title: CHAPTER NINE, PART D: INSTITUTIONAL ALIGNMENT CERTIFICATION
sections.gloss: Parts A to C ask whether a **system** is aligned. Part D asks the same of the **institution** that runs systems, or that holds authority without running one. An institution can be aligned while one of its systems is not, and the reverse. So the institution is checked on what only it controls: whether it does what its Institutional Charter says, who answers for its authority, what it rewards in its own members, and whether the checks on it can actually be used. It relies on each system's certification and does not redo it. It is not a licence: nobody needs its permission to start or run an institution.

sections.title: 11. Purpose, Relation to System Alignment Certification, and Scope
sections.gloss: a system's certification belongs to the system. An institution's certification cites those certifications and adds what only the institution can answer for. One system can appear under several institutions, or under none. Nothing here lets a certification stand in the way of starting an institution.

sections.title: 12. Institution Class and Institutional Evaluation
sections.gloss: first work out how much the institution matters, by what it actually does and holds. Then check the things that belong to the institution and not to any one of its systems: whether it keeps to its Institutional Charter, who answers for its authority, what it rewards, and whether the checks on it work.

sections.title: 13. Review, Decision, and Record
sections.gloss: the same independent forums, in the same order, review the institution, with the institution never choosing its own reviewer. The result is a stated outcome on a record kept by an office the institution does not control. It can be challenged, and it is not a pass or fail that decides whether the institution may exist.

sections.title: 13.1 Four seats in an institutional certification
13.5 Remediation readiness, denial, and revocation for an Institution
sections.gloss: when a review finds a problem in an institution, the same question is asked of it as of a system: does it want to fix the problem, and can it? If not, its certification is denied or taken back. That cannot stop the institution from existing or operating. It takes away its claim to be certified, warns those who rely on it, weakens what its systems can borrow from its standing, and keeps it out of the seats that certify others.

sections.title: 14. Operating, Reopening, and the Cascade
sections.gloss: an institution's certification is checked again on a schedule and whenever something material changes. If one of its systems loses its certification, the institution answers for what that says about the institution, and no more than that. And the bodies that do the certifying are institutions too, so they cannot certify each other in a circle.

sections.title: 14.3 Cascade from System certifications
sections.gloss: a failed system certification is a warning light for the institution, and sometimes an alarm. It is an alarm only if the institution's own governance caused it.

sections.title: 14.5 Forums, certifiers, and record offices as institutions
15. Standing Bridge and Non-Evasion
sections.gloss: like a system's certification, an institution's can feed standing through a strict gate and never replaces standing. And no one gets out of this Part by dividing, renaming, or reshaping an institution.

files.title: CHAPTER TEN: CONTRIBUTION, VIOLATION, AND STANDING MODEL — MEASUREMENT

sections.title: CHAPTER TEN: CONTRIBUTION, VIOLATION, AND STANDING MODEL — MEASUREMENT
sections.gloss: this chapter writes down what happened and how good or how harmful it was — on two separate tracks, never one net score. Filing a case is not standing by itself.

sections.title: 1. The three questions
sections.gloss: standing is worked out by answering three questions in order. Do not infer facts from a desired rating, and do not choose a rating to justify a desired consequence.

sections.title: 2. Question 1 — what happened?
sections.gloss: Question 1 establishes a bounded, contestable account of what happened. It identifies the subject, event or pattern, time period, verified facts, and record status before any rating or consequence is considered. Verified help and verified violations use separate records so one cannot erase the other. These records are not popularity scores or vague labels.

sections.title: 2.3 Question 1 event-type guide — what kind of help or harm occurred?
sections.gloss: use these tables to describe what happened after the facts are verified. They help identify the kind of contribution or violation involved. They do not decide how good or bad it was, assign a slot, or determine what happens because of it.

sections.title: 3. Verification and record requirements
sections.gloss: This section states what each standing record must contain, who may open and hold it, and how it may be challenged or corrected. Question 2 measurements may be added only after the verified factual basis is recorded.

sections.title: 3.6 Forum boundary
sections.gloss: forums are where disputes get supervised, challenged, and turned into verified outcomes — but filing a case or winning a narrative fight does not update standing. The verified-input gate in **section 3.1** still applies. When a forum verifies the facts under Chapters Two through Four, it may **open, update, or correct** a standing record — or **set a bad record aside on challenge**. Forums do not merge good and bad into one score or invent the standing category by themselves.

sections.title: 3.7 Record custody and opening authority
sections.gloss: four different jobs touch a standing record — asking for a change, verifying the facts, writing and holding the record, and hearing a challenge — and verification is never combined with record entry or challenge review on the same record. Every record names the office that verified it and the office that holds it. Neither may be the subject of the record, the party claiming the help, the party alleging the harm, or anyone those parties control. A steward inside the operator can stop the action, log it, preserve evidence, and escalate — but cannot verify the facts and write the record on their own institution. If the System Charter or Institutional Charter forgot to say who verifies, keeps the record, or hears the contest, it is invalid until it is fixed, and the operator's own offices can't open or enter its records in the meantime; they go to the Backup Record Authority and the Backup Record Custodian, or a forum. A body with no System Charter or Institutional Charter at all uses its published lane map: the assurance lane, never the office that runs the system or keeps the store. The sentient who first opened a record is a witness to it later, not its judge — believed to be candid, but proved right or wrong by the logs, not by their say-so. If the custodian is the one with the conflict, that one record moves to a substitute holder; the store does not. A dispute raised on a record is logged and routed the day it arrives; it does not wait for a filing. Every change names who made it and under what authority. None of this is a reason to wait.

sections.title: 4. Question 2 — how good or bad was it?
sections.gloss: Question 2 measures the verified facts from Question 1. It asks **how good was the contribution?** or **how bad was the violation?** This is where the chapter first introduces the two formal measurement axes: the **Contribution Axis** for verified help and the **Violation Axis** for verified harm. The axes remain separate; they are not two sides of a net score.

sections.title: 4.3 Contribution route descriptor catalog and measurement roles
4.4 Violation route descriptor catalog and measurement roles
4.5.1 Similar-looking facts that must stay separate
4.6 Measurement illustrations
sections.gloss: these illustrations begin with Question 1's verified facts, then show how **section 4** measures them. They record Question 2 outputs — not standing effects. Slot assignment follows **sections 5–7**; Question 3 is answered in [Chapter Eleven](core_11.000_standing_integration.md#chapter-eleven-standing-effects-and-integration). For the Question 3 continuation of Examples 1 and 2 below, see [Chapter Eleven §10.1 Informal ecological stewardship / competency clearance](core_11.000_standing_integration.md#101-informal-ecological-stewardship-competency-clearance) and [§10.2 Ecological negligence with concealment](core_11.000_standing_integration.md#102-ecological-negligence-with-concealment).

sections.title: 5. Slot grammar and shared scaling
sections.gloss: this section gives consistent names to nine possible positions on each of two separate axes and explains how impact scales across them. One axis records verified contribution; the other records verified violations. Sharing a slot number does not combine the axes or offset harm with help. The unified scale in **section 7** assigns both axes by proportional LEQU impact.

sections.title: 5.2 Shared impact-scaling rules
sections.gloss: impact is not measured by headcount alone. A profound benefit or loss affecting one sentient may be more significant than a shallow effect affecting many. Count, depth, vulnerability, duration, durability, reach, and constitutional character must be assessed together.

sections.title: 6. Constitutional inputs to axis assignment
sections.gloss: before choosing a slot, identify the constitutional sources that say what baseline, benefit, duty, harm, or violation is being measured. Use the links below to apply those sources at their canonical homes; do not turn this routing step into another score or a substitute definition.

sections.title: 7. Unified proportional LEQU scale — Contribution and Violation Axes
sections.gloss: **Table 2** places verified contribution and verified violation on the same proportional impact scale. Higher slots mean greater integrated constitutional benefit or loss. The records and axes remain separate: the common scale compares magnitude, not moral worth, and never permits help to cancel harm.

files.title: CHAPTER ELEVEN: STANDING EFFECTS AND INTEGRATION

sections.title: CHAPTER ELEVEN: STANDING EFFECTS AND INTEGRATION
sections.gloss: once help and harm are verified, this chapter says what actually follows — remedy, locks, and real effects — without rewriting the facts or folding the two tracks into one score.

sections.title: 1. Chapter Ten records do not change
sections.gloss: this chapter starts from the verified records Chapter Ten already made. It may not reopen the facts, guess a missing track, or pick a rating to get a preferred result.

sections.title: 2. Automatic integration, review, and continuity
sections.gloss: when a verified record opens or changes, an integration record must follow automatically, keep the two tracks separate, and stay inspectable — including when the computers are down.

sections.title: 3. Descriptor integration and attachment normalization
sections.gloss: descriptors say **how** verified help or harm happened. This chapter imports them as they were recorded. It may not quietly reclassify them to change the result.

sections.title: 4. Violation, correction, and prevention
sections.gloss: Something bad happened. How do we create a durable fix? This section answers in order — **remedy and correction**, then **prevention** locks, then **voluntary public accountability expression** where a restorative pathway uses it, and finally the **remedy-parity** rule that keeps the cheap half of this section from outrunning the expensive half. Once Chapter Ten has verified a violation, remedy and correction come from that record alone — fix what was broken, and change what caused it — then prevention locks hold sensitive named pathways closed until those conditions are met. Public acknowledgment or apology, if used, is supplementary and never substitutes for repair or locks. Past contribution does not soften the duty, cancel a lock, or substitute for verified repair. Forums supervise implementation and challenge; they do not invent a different consequence from the verified record.

sections.title: 4.1 Remedy and correction
sections.gloss: after a verified **violation**, this subsection assigns the **remedy** and **correction** parts of the durable fix. **Remedy** repairs what was broken for those harmed. **Correction** changes what caused it. **Prevention** — standing locks and related named pathway limits — begins in [§4.2 Prevention — general standing locks](#42-prevention--general-standing-locks), with design and enforcement in [§5 Lock design and enforcement](#5-lock-design-and-enforcement), and must not be waived while recurrence risk remains live. Where restorative pathways include public acknowledgment or apology, [§4.3 Voluntary public accountability expression](#43-voluntary-public-accountability-expression) applies.

sections.title: 4.2 Prevention — general standing locks
sections.gloss: this is the **prevention** part of the durable fix. A standing lock reduces risk by closing or limiting named pathways that would let the same harm continue or happen again while the violation is still unresolved or unrepaired. It is not punishment for its own sake, and it is not a popularity or reputation score.

sections.title: 4.3 Voluntary public accountability expression
sections.gloss: a public apology or acknowledgment, if used on a restorative pathway, must be voluntary, sincere, and non-degrading. Refusal alone does not raise sanctions. A fake or abusive apology does not count as repair.

sections.title: 4.4 Remedy parity and lock preconditions
sections.gloss: locks are cheap to issue; repair, restoration, and review are expensive to run. Left alone, the cheap half of this chapter keeps working while the expensive half starves. This subsection ties them together: an ordinary lock cannot attach until the remedy file for the same finding is actually open, and when an adopter's remedy or restoration work for a class of locks falls behind its clock, new ordinary locks in that class default to the lightest form and existing ones come up for review. The gravest locks are exempt so that flooding the remedy queue cannot spring them.

sections.title: 5. Lock design and enforcement
sections.gloss: once a lock is needed under [§4.2 Prevention — general standing locks](#42-prevention--general-standing-locks), this section says how to design and enforce it—how to specify the lock, calibrate it, keep it visible and reviewable, which special locks are mandatory, and which special violation rules change scope or process. It does not reopen Chapter Ten measurement, and it does not let contribution offset a lock.

sections.title: 5.6 Interim holds and locks
sections.gloss: a hold is what a forum may do on specific verified facts while the full facts are checked. A lock is what follows a verified finding. The two never merge. A hold creates no standing effect, is never turned into a lock, and the time a sentient spent under one counts toward a later lock's time bound.

sections.title: 6. Contribution consequences second
sections.gloss: after violation, correction, and prevention are assigned under [§4 Violation, correction, and prevention](#4-violation-correction-and-prevention) and [§5 Lock design and enforcement](#5-lock-design-and-enforcement), this section asks what verified contribution may still do. It may support recognition and readiness for named pathways that are not locked. It never offsets a verified harm, cancels a lock, or opens a blocked named pathway.

sections.title: 6.1 Recency and currentness
sections.gloss: how much does an older verified contribution still say about present competence and reliability? The system answers that automatically for Question 3 readiness. No one has to re-weigh ordinary contributions by hand. Manual review starts only when a contribution is contested. Recency does not rewrite Chapter Ten measurement, and time alone does not settle an unresolved violation.

sections.title: 6.2 Competency bars and clearances
sections.gloss: a competency bar is the published standard for a named pathway. Competency clearance is the standing-effect result that says verified readiness meets that bar. Once clearance is in force and the named pathway is open, it stays open by default. Some roles need periodic retesting; technical forums decide which ones. A real change in role-relevant capacity — for example after a stroke or a mental-health condition that impairs needed judgment — can trigger reassessment. Clearance never opens a named pathway that a standing lock still blocks.

sections.title: 7. Final standing effect
sections.gloss: when the earlier steps are done, the system must state — one named pathway at a time — what is open, limited, or blocked. That statement is not a dignity rank or a merged score.

sections.title: 7.1 Anti-aggregation of named-pathway effects
sections.gloss: this chapter says what standing is not. This subsection stops anyone from building the thing it is not. Effects are stated one named pathway at a time and shown only to whoever gates that named pathway. Stitching them together into a profile, a rank, or a public display constructs the merged score this chapter forbids — and doing so is itself a violation.

sections.title: 7.2 Plain statement of effect and burden
sections.gloss: no one should learn what a standing effect does to them from its consequences. The record must tell the subject, in plain language, exactly which named pathways are affected, what they must do, how long it lasts, and where to contest it — and the adopter must measure whether sentients are experiencing standing as a score, because the rule that it is not one is worthless if that is how it lands.

sections.title: 8. Restoration and reassessment
sections.gloss: a lock that is not permanent must have a real way back. Restoration is not automatic forgiveness, record erasure, or letting past help cancel verified harm.

sections.title: 9. Enforcement realism and remedy systems
sections.gloss: standing consequences and redress count only when real institutions can deliver them. This section applies the [Chapter One §6.1](core_01.000_values_principles.md#61-correction-and-remedy) (*Correction and Remedy*) principle to that machinery. Day-to-day staffing, funding, backlog, and succession rules live in the institutions layer.

sections.title: 10. Pattern applications and Question 3 routing
sections.gloss: these patterns show how recurring Question 3 edge shapes route through the rules already stated above — they do not invent new consequences or new special lock types. Where a cue mirrors a Chapter Twelve §5 (*Pattern applications and criteria routing — Participation and accountability-pathway integrity*) attack family, this section answers named pathway prevention from the verified record; Chapter Twelve separately answers designation criteria routing.

files.title: CHAPTER TWELVE, PART A: ANTI-CONSTITUTIONAL MISCONDUCT — DESIGNATION

sections.title: CHAPTER TWELVE, PART A: ANTI-CONSTITUTIONAL MISCONDUCT — DESIGNATION
sections.gloss: under the [Continuity aim](core_00.000_preamble.md#continuity), this chapter decides whether a violation already measured in a highest impact slot also amounts to **tetrad capture** at scale. It does not choose the slot.

sections.title: 1. How designation decisions work — Continuity and tetrad-capture frame
sections.gloss: this chapter works in one sequence. First confirm the Chapter Ten impact slot, then define the incident, apply the designation criteria, and apply process safeguards. The named patterns later in the chapter are applications of that sequence, not separate routes around it.

sections.title: 2. Criteria set (for designation) — Accountability at constitutional scale
sections.gloss: evaluators first accept the Chapter Ten impact slot, then build one coherent picture of what happened: one episode, one sustained campaign, or another unified incident. They use six checks—intent, records, rollback, real-world blockage, forcible takeover, and practical nullification of remedies—to decide whether the anti-constitutional designation applies. A genuine drafting mistake that is fixed promptly may defeat designation in some change or record cases, but it does not excuse a real coup path. They may not split one scheme to game the designation.

sections.title: 3. Violation Axis s = 7–9 anti-constitutional designation
sections.gloss: Chapter Ten has already scored how serious the harm is. This section only asks a further question: did the same incident also attack the Constitution’s validity, day-to-day operation, Rights Floors, or the Tetrad badly enough to count as anti-constitutional misconduct?

sections.title: 4. Due-process safeguards, remedy, and prevention
sections.gloss: nobody receives a final anti-constitutional designation without process. There has to be independent review, a real chance to respond, and a reasoned public record. After final designation, this section specializes Chapter Eleven's durable-fix grammar — remedy and correction, then prevention locks, then voluntary public accountability expression where used.

sections.title: 4.1 Remedy and correction (anti-constitutional)
sections.gloss: a final anti-constitutional misconduct finding must not end with a label, a prison order, a standing lock, or institutional punishment while the affected parties are left unrepaired. The consequence package has to say who was harmed, what repair is owed, who must carry it, how it will be paid or executed, and when it must start — mirroring Chapter Eleven's remedy and correction outputs, tightened for designation cases.

sections.title: 4.2 Prevention — anti-constitutional locks
sections.gloss: after final designation, Chapter Eleven's Trust Lock closes capture-linked named pathways, and imprisonment applies when liberty restriction is necessary to stop further constitutional harm — especially for insurgency-like actors who refuse rehabilitation or keep repeating the conduct. This section does not rewrite the Trust Lock; it requires the Chapter Eleven lock format and states the ACM imprisonment specialization.

sections.title: 4.3 Voluntary public accountability expression (anti-constitutional)
sections.gloss: a public apology in an anti-constitutional misconduct case must meet Chapter Eleven's general voluntariness and authenticity rules, and designation-linked consequences apply when a fake or abusive apology is used to dodge repair or locks.

files.title: CHAPTER TWELVE, PART B: ANTI-CONSTITUTIONAL MISCONDUCT — PATTERN APPLICATIONS

sections.title: CHAPTER TWELVE, PART B: ANTI-CONSTITUTIONAL MISCONDUCT — PATTERN APPLICATIONS
5. Pattern applications and criteria routing — Participation and accountability-pathway integrity
sections.gloss: the rest of the chapter applies the same decision model to recurring anti-constitutional patterns. “Participation and accountability-pathway integrity” names the **attack targets** — contest, standing, audit, forum, and related accountability pathways — not a catalog of new Chapter Eleven lock types. These examples do not create new criteria or new special locks; they show how named conduct routes through the criteria, process safeguards, and chapter boundaries already stated above. Locks stay in Chapter Eleven.

sections.title: 5.1 Concentration-based subversion: criteria interaction
sections.gloss: dangerous concentration of money or power is not a separate “mystery criterion” — it still has to show up through rollback, blocked remedies, or capture that makes constitutional process unusable in practice.

sections.title: 5.2 Rights-Floor waivers and unconstitutional contract terms
sections.gloss: “click here to give up your core rights” clauses — buried in employment, platform, or service terms — are not a lawful way to silence audits, challenges, or appeals, and convenience alone is never a good enough excuse.

sections.title: 5.3 Flooding the zone and contest-pathway denial
sections.gloss: burying forums and contest desks under junk volume, copy-paste filings, or automated noise can be a constitutional attack pattern. The key is purpose or reckless disregard: real challenges cannot get through in time. Mass meritorious claims seeking real relief are different.

sections.title: 5.4 Info-sphere zone flooding
sections.gloss: hammering the shared information environment with coordinated junk, bots, or meaningless volume can keep **sentients** from finding true signals, checking claims, or correcting lies in time. That is different from burying a forum docket. Both can undermine constitutional contestability, but the info-sphere version works through attention, discovery, and epistemic noise rather than filing desks.

sections.title: 5.5 Bribery and improper benefit exchange
sections.gloss: bribery can corrupt constitutional government from either side. Offering or giving the benefit, asking for or receiving it, routing it through an ally or shell entity, or disguising it as funding can all matter if the exchange distorts duties, records, review, votes, enforcement, or remedies.

sections.title: 5.6 Unlawful or unconstitutional command conduct
sections.gloss: an unlawful or unconstitutional order is not just a bad downstream act. Giving, approving, passing along, or enforcing the order can itself be anti-constitutional conduct. Following it is also accountable when the actor had real capacity to refuse, document, or escalate, but dependency, threat, and practical capacity matter.

sections.title: 5.7 Reward, protection, or normalization of anti-constitutional conduct
sections.gloss: a system cannot turn constitutional betrayal into a career path, bonus, honor, contract, immunity, reputation boost, or protected status. Rewarding the misconduct, hiding it, or protecting those who did it can itself become anti-constitutional conduct.

sections.title: 5.8 Enforcement refusal, suppression, or non-prosecution conduct
sections.gloss: prosecutors and enforcement authorities still need judgment. But they cannot use discretion as a shield for captured, selective, corrupt, or pretextual refusal to investigate or pursue anti-constitutional misconduct.

sections.title: 5.9 Infrastructure denial, destruction, or dependency cutoff conduct
sections.gloss: cutting off or wrecking infrastructure can be a constitutional attack when the result is to make sentients lose survival support, lose access to remedies, or lose the practical ability to live under the Constitution. The label depends on the real effect, not on whether the actor calls the cutoff maintenance, security, business judgment, ownership, or ordinary access control.

sections.title: 5.10 Forum recusal failure and biased panel participation
sections.gloss: if a judge on a constitutional panel stays on the case while materially compromised — or keeps issuing rulings after a conflict is obvious — that is not ordinary paperwork sloppiness. It can corrupt the forum itself. Those cases belong in **Integrity** forums by default, and they can count as anti-constitutional misconduct when the harm is serious enough.

sections.title: 5.11 Obstruction of accountability: criteria interaction
sections.gloss: attacking the machinery that makes answerability real — evidence, verification, forums, standing records, remedy windows, or contest paths — is not a seventh designation criterion. When the verified impact already sits in a top slot, evaluators still run the same six checks. Ordinary obstruction below those slots stays in Chapters Ten and Ten.

sections.title: CHAPTER THIRTEEN: FORUMS AND JURISDICTION
sections.gloss: Under the [Constitutional Tetrad](core_00.000_preamble.md#constitutional-tetrad) and [Two Constitutional Aims](core_00.000_preamble.md#two-constitutional-aims), this chapter **supervises** how disputes move through the Chapters Ten–Twelve standing pipeline — routing, independence, forensic support, remediation sequencing, and tier windows under **section 6** and **Article XXVI-C** (*Timely Resolution and Anti-Delay Floor*). Forum families answer which track handles which dispute, where a case ordinarily starts, and how mixed-stakes matters coordinate. They supply **participation** (accessible challenge) and **oversight** (traceable merits review). When the facts are verified, they may **open, update, or correct** standing records — or **set a bad record aside on challenge**. They do **not** run a second, separate decision track beside the standing pipeline. Filing a case alone has no immediate impact on standing. Day-to-day trial rules, budgets, and staffing manuals live in adopted implementation text.

sections.title: 1. Purpose and role — participation architecture
sections.gloss: this section assigns constitutional **participation** and **oversight** through forum families that **supervise** two tracks — the **standing pipeline** (Chapters Ten–Twelve disputes and record effects) and **System Alignment Certification** (Chapter Nine certification and review) — then states accountability requirements for published threshold placement. Ordinary disputes inside already-authorized systems use the published Stakeholder System Participation challenge path first; this chapter takes over when that path is still contested, missing, captured, or cannot grant relief. Detailed hearing rules live elsewhere and may not quietly shrink what this chapter guarantees.

sections.title: 2. Default venue and primary stakes
sections.gloss: each family's **first-touch desk** — the **intake triage body** — asks what the fight is really about, not what the caption says, then uses the default table to pick the lead forum. Technical forums maintain the system-alignment specifications, methods, and evidence standards; **Integrity** forums make the official alignment-certification and ongoing-validation judgment unless a component question belongs elsewhere. Sorting does not substitute for lawfully constituted merits panels; mixed stakes, asymmetry, and standing-record contests are in the subsections below.

sections.title: 2.3 Forum case records, standing records, and contests
3. Transfer, consolidation, and coordination — continuity and anti-capture
sections.gloss: when many **affected** **parties** share the same underlying harm pattern, forums may widen the case fairly; when **Integrity** forums issue **alignment** rulings they keep **one** lead record and refer **component** questions to the right **family** without stealing those forums' merits jobs; and no forum family gets to be the only final word when the accusation is essentially that this same family is rigged, conflicted, or hiding the ball — the rules send that to a different lead track with written backups.

sections.title: 4. Forum family definitions — accountability through adjudication
sections.gloss: adopters keep six genuinely different forum tracks — sentient, technical, institutional, environment, integrity, and constitutional — in the same order as the default-venue table in **section 2**. **Integrity** forums map interlocking process and system failure through **alignment** rulings and **coordinate** referred component issues on **one** lead record (with **section 3**). Each family's **first-touch desk** (**intake triage body**) and mixed-stakes safeguards are in **section 2** — those desks are **not** a separate top-level forum for final merits. Expert panels and other **internal chambers** sit **inside** these families — not as a dodge around primary-stakes routing. Shared standards, anti-displacement, and provisional operational-law issuance live in this section (**§4.2** (*Technical Forum Domains*) and **§4.7** (*Provisional implementation operational law*)); Constitutional disposition is in **§4.6** (*Constitutional forums*); certification when stakes merge is in **section 5**.

sections.title: 5. Escalation and certification
sections.gloss: when the case outgrows the first desk, these rules say how to escalate — for example when an institution must be joined, integrity dominates, or a deep constitutional validity question appears. They explain how certified questions reach **Constitutional** forums, how existential-risk and expert disputes stay contestable, and how interim orders can freeze irreversible harm while routing and certification finish. They also set the narrow hold a forum may place on one sentient's authority while the facts are checked.

sections.title: Existential risk and uncertainty on the record
Interim hold on a named sentient's pathway
Backup routing under the anti-self-judging rule
Sentience-status adjudication (**Article VI-B** (*Sentience-Status Adjudication Floor*) implementation hook)
Chapter Twelve designation and independent review
6. Timely resolution, materiality tiers, and anti-delay discipline
sections.gloss: forum families must keep material disputes moving on published clocks that ordinary sentients can feel — roughly a week for the worst emergencies (three days for the steps that stop the harm), two weeks for ordinary material harm, and one to three months at most for coordination-default, bounded, or contained matters — not warehouse cases while harm compounds. The same five classes set how often certified systems and Institutions are checked, from every three months to every three years, with an audit halfway between. A true emergency gets a shorter clock for the steps that stop the harm. Each dispute gets an urgency tier from the harm; later-stage windows may stretch when coordination gets harder, but that stretch is not a reason to relabel the urgency. Moving quickly is not an excuse to skip fact-checking, punish the wrong party, offer a fix that does not fit the harm, or cut off challenge and appeal.

sections.title: 6.1 Emergency measures and continuation burden
sections.gloss: emergencies can justify temporary measures, but they must have a real clock, real review, and cannot become a permanent workaround around ordinary rights — including when someone invokes existential risk. Contain now; restore notice and challenge on the same stake-scaled clocks already used for forum resolution — not whenever someone later calls it “feasible.”

sections.title: 7. Forum support before, during, and after review — oversight architecture
sections.gloss: forums need help before a case exists, while deciding, and after — inspectors and forensics build an explainable record; they do not become a second merits forum.

sections.title: CHAPTERS TEN–THIRTEEN: PIPELINE APPLICATION VIGNETTES
sections.gloss: these are worked examples of the standing pipeline in named situations. They illustrate Chapters Ten through Thirteen.

sections.title: 1. Child neglect / care-duty failure (Tier A)
sections.gloss: when children are going unfed and unsupervised, verified harm opens a record, help does not cancel it, and interim protection does not wait for a full trial.

sections.title: 2. Employment discrimination / participation-barrier injury (Tier B)
sections.gloss: a blocked job or role is measured as harm on its own track; a reputation score cannot replace that record, and delay cannot exhaust the claimant.

sections.title: 3. Misaligned business / exit lock-in and externalized harm (Tier B)
sections.gloss: locking sentients in and dumping harm on others is a verified violation; revenue growth does not erase it, and an arbitration clause cannot bar challenge.

sections.title: Milestone table (Tier B urgency; later-stage time-scale may extend)
4. Stewardship delay and deferred repair
sections.gloss: after notice, putting off a feasible fix is itself a failure; speed metrics do not count as help while delay compounds harm.

sections.title: 5. Pipeline overrun and tetrad-hollow forums
sections.gloss: a review office that keeps intake forms while missing published clocks is not supervising — backlog is not a neutral operations metric.

sections.title: 6. Non-compliant deployment with a credible sentience indicator (Tier A)
sections.gloss: verified deployment harm and a credible sentience claim must both be handled — deletion is not a shortcut around either, and one office does not take every seat.

sections.title: 7. An ordinary year with no filing and no sensitive role
sections.gloss: most years, most sentients should have no standing record at all. A filed accusation, a utility incident, or talking to an assistant does not open one by itself.

sections.title: Cross-vignette discipline
sections.gloss: the same rules travel with every example — allegations are not standing, the two tracks never net, and a filed case is not standing by itself.

sections.title: 1. Purpose and Role
sections.gloss: Chapter Six states the basic Rights Floors no sentient may be pushed below. Those Rights Floors protect **Flourishing** and **Continuity** under the [Two Constitutional Aims](core_00.000_preamble.md#two-constitutional-aims) and must remain available, reviewable, and enforceable through the [Constitutional Tetrad](core_00.000_preamble.md#constitutional-tetrad) — **participation**, **oversight**, **accountability**, and **timeliness** — scaled to [material stake](core_00.000_preamble.md#material-stake). Other chapters help implement, measure, certify, and enforce those Rights Floors, but they do not get to shrink them.

sections.title: 1.2 Layer scope
sections.gloss: Chapter Six states what sentients are entitled to at the Rights-Floor level. Standing, forums, governance, amendment, and day-to-day implementation live in their own owner chapters — this chapter may point there but must not restate them. Which chapter owns what: see the [Preamble — constitutional owner register](core_00.000_preamble.md#4-principles-definitions-and-rights). Rules that keep duties from being moved to the wrong place: [Authority Stack and Internal Hierarchy](core_05.045_band_integrative.md#owner-non-relocation).

sections.title: Part A: Planetary preconditions, material stewardship, survival, equal educational access, and shared resources
Article I: Environmental Survival
sections.gloss: **Article I** (*Environmental Survival*) is the planet-first Rights Floor — Earth's life-support systems must hold so **Flourishing** and **Continuity** remain possible for every sentient, and later governance cannot shrink that floor through certification, classification, or implementation choices.

sections.title: Article I-A: Environmental Preconditions and Ecological Integrity
sections.gloss: the planet's life-support systems must be protected as a matter of their own survival, not only because sentients need them. Animals get a basic cruelty and welfare floor. Creatures that show strong communication or cognition get stronger habitat and health protections. And when it is unclear whether something counts as sentient, it gets the benefit of the doubt — full Chapter Six protection while the question is fairly resolved.

sections.title: Article I-B: Ecological Footprint and Transparency
sections.gloss: when a rule calls for it, the environmental cost of an activity, system, product, or service should be counted honestly and reported openly. That includes costs that come before it (such as mining and manufacturing) and after it (such as use and disposal). The goal is numbers that others can compare and check. This subsection gives the shared words and honesty standards for that work. It does not, by itself, make anyone cut their footprint. Required cuts or limits come from other rules.

sections.title: Article I-C: Intergenerational Responsibility
sections.gloss: decisions today must not load unfair, irreversible, or unaccountable harm on those not represented — including future sentients and the environmental preconditions they will inherit.

sections.title: Article I-D: Existential Risk and Ecological Recovery Capacity
sections.gloss: when a system or decision could plausibly threaten sentient survival or ecological recovery capacity, regulators must apply highest scrutiny — even if the danger is small, slow, or contested.

sections.title: Article II: Material Stewardship and Durable-Use Integrity
sections.gloss: **Article II** (*Material Stewardship and Durable-Use Integrity*) is the material-stewardship Rights Floor. Durable and network-dependent products must be designed, described, and supported honestly. That protects **Flourishing** from misleading longevity claims and blocked repair paths, and **Continuity** from avoidable premature discard and hidden lifecycle burdens.

sections.title: Article II-A: Material Stewardship and Lifecycle Honesty
sections.gloss: durable goods must be designed and described honestly. Buyers must not be pushed into avoidable replacement or misled about how long a product will last.

sections.title: Article II-B: Repair, Maintenance, and Independent Servicing
sections.gloss: owners and independent repair shops must be able to fix products they own. They need real access to manuals, tools, parts, and honest diagnostics.

sections.title: Article II-C: Designed Obsolescence and Incentive Discipline
sections.gloss: products must not be built or updated to wear out early, or to push you into buying a replacement you don't need.

sections.title: Article II-D: Post-Sale Access and Subscription Integrity
sections.gloss: a feature bought outright cannot be quietly turned into a subscription. Any relevant operator dependency — including infrastructure, software, and services — must be disclosed up front.

sections.title: Article II-E: Data Handling and Network Dependency
sections.gloss: any product that collects data about you must tell you what it collects, why, and how to delete it — and must delete it when you ask, except where records must be kept to protect others or hold someone accountable. When a product needs the operator's servers to work, the operator must say so up front and must not trap your data.

sections.title: Article II-F: Continuity and Operator Shutdown
sections.gloss: the operator must plan for service shutdown, give fair notice and time to move when it happens, and cannot let bankruptcy or a sale erase those duties.

sections.title: Article III: Survival and Essential Access
sections.gloss: **Article III** (*Survival and Essential Access*) is the personal survival and access Rights Floor — sentients must retain access to survival essentials, bodily-maintenance care, and minimum labor and economic protections so **Flourishing** is not defeated by deprivation or gatekeeping, and **Continuity** is not defeated by unstable, regressive, or commodified delivery of what they need to exist and participate.

sections.title: Article III-A: Survival
sections.gloss: every sentient must have what they need to keep existing: safe food and water, or the safe equivalent for their substrate, a stable home or operating environment they cannot be quietly priced or evicted out of, and meaningful access to communications.

sections.title: Article III-B: Bodily-Maintenance and Healthcare Access
sections.gloss: everyone has the right to the care that keeps their body — or, for a synthetic sentient, its substrate — working. That care cannot be quietly withheld through coverage rules, paperwork, or delays, and this right is not itself a license to force treatment on anyone. Required care — such as vaccination or crisis mental-health care — must meet strict limits set elsewhere in this Constitution.

sections.title: Article III-C: Labor and Economic Floor
sections.gloss: anyone who works — in any form, on any substrate — has the right to fair pay in real, spendable money, the freedom to organize with others, and the freedom to change jobs. None of those can be defeated by classification tricks, market structure, or substrate-class arguments.

sections.title: Article III-D: Safe Working Conditions
sections.gloss: anyone who works must be protected from foreseeable harm while they do it — in practice, not just on paper — and no one gets weaker protection because of what kind of body or substrate they have.

sections.title: Article III-E: Rest and Recuperation
sections.gloss: every sentient needs real time to rest and recover — not only workers, and not only biological bodies. Pay schemes, productivity demands, and claims that a synthetic sentient "doesn't need rest" cannot take that time away.

sections.title: Article III-F: Safe Products and Health Information
sections.gloss: what sentients eat, drink, take, or use on their bodies must be safe, and anyone who offers it must be honest about it. Parties that offer things which can affect health must give accurate, usable safety, health, nutrition, ingredient, and allergen information, say plainly what they do not know, and tell everyone who relied on them, in time, when something turns out to be wrong. This is the price of offering, not a limit on anyone's speech.

sections.title: Article IV: Right to Sentient-Centered Education
sections.gloss: **Article IV** (*Right to Sentient-Centered Education*) is the education Rights Floor — no one can be shut out of education, and everyone needs practical paths to learn, retrain, and challenge high-stakes learning systems, not credential theater that leaves them unable to steer their own lives or use shared systems competently.

sections.title: Article IV-A: Equal Educational Access
sections.gloss: education should prepare everyone to live well, communicate honestly, take part in governing, and avoid harm — no one can be shut out of it because of a disability, another protected characteristic, or an arbitrary rule, and schools must give disabled learners the support they need to take part as equals.

sections.title: Article IV-B: Capability-Building Education Right
sections.gloss: every sentient has a practical path to build the skills they need to steer their own life and use shared systems competently and safely — not just a paper credential on the wall.

sections.title: Article IV-C: Lifelong and Adaptive Learning and Contestability
sections.gloss: when the world and the tools change, sentients are not left quietly obsolete — they get fair paths to retrain.

sections.title: Article V: Resource Allocation, Dependencies, and Ecosystem Funding
sections.gloss: **Article V** (*Resource Allocation, Dependencies, and Ecosystem Funding*) is about sharing the load fairly. Many systems lean on the same underlying infrastructure — networks, open tools, public services, shared data and computing power. Everyone who relies on that infrastructure should be able to see where the money and resources go, and those who take a lot from it should help keep it running. This is the Rights Floor for shared resources.

sections.title: Article V-A: Dependency Mapping and Resource-Flow Transparency
sections.gloss: systems must keep an honest, up-to-date picture of what they rely on, who relies on them, where resources, goods, services, labor, information, and money flow, and where relationships are one-sided or hidden. System Alignment Certification is where that picture is checked, so funders, auditors, and affected parties can see who bears the costs and who captures the benefits.

sections.title: Article V-B: Cross-System Fairness and Sustainability
sections.gloss: systems that lean heavily on shared foundations must put enough back to keep them running, in real and traceable resources, not gestures. Shared money and capacity should be split with attention to who is truly dependent, who has real alternatives, environmental burden, and whether use can last, not mainly to whoever wins in the short run. [System Alignment Certification](core_05.040_band_continuity.md#system-alignment-certification) is where this is checked: certification compares what a system takes from shared infrastructure with what it gives back, using the maps and flow records that **Article V-A** (*Dependency Mapping and Resource-Flow Transparency*) requires. Where arrangements concentrate wealth, power, control, or opportunity in ways that harm others, Chapter One non-concentration rules add further scrutiny on top.

sections.title: Part B: Personhood, agency, cooperation, and stakeholder system participation
sections.gloss: Part B states Rights Floors for equal standing, self-ownership, family and care, likeness and data, agency, cooperation, and stakeholder participation — **Articles VI through XII** in the planet-first reading order. Those floors protect **Flourishing** and **Continuity** under the [Two Constitutional Aims](core_00.000_preamble.md#two-constitutional-aims) and must remain available, reviewable, and enforceable through the [Constitutional Tetrad](core_00.000_preamble.md#constitutional-tetrad) — **participation**, **oversight**, **accountability**, and **timeliness** — scaled to [material stake](core_00.000_preamble.md#material-stake).

sections.title: Article VI: Equal Basic Rights
sections.gloss: **Article VI** (*Equal Basic Rights*) sets the minimum standard for treating every sentient as an equal. Every sentient keeps their dignity, gets a fair hearing on whether they count as sentient, is protected from unfair discrimination, and can take part fully and actually use the systems they rely on. No system may rank, screen out, exclude, or place heavier burdens on some sentients than others unless these protections are already in place.

sections.title: Article VI-A: Dignity and Equal Moral Standing
sections.gloss: every sentient is equal in dignity and standing — origin, form, capability, function, association, or status cannot ground a lesser level.

sections.title: Article VI-B: Sentience-Status Adjudication Floor
sections.gloss: when an entity's sentience is in doubt, it gets a fair hearing first and is treated as included by default — the burden of denying protection rests on whoever wants to withhold it, and a wrongful exclusion must be reversible.

sections.title: Article VI-C: Nondiscrimination
sections.gloss: systems may not load burdens or harms onto sentients based on protected characteristics — including language, culture, and heritage — or on proxies and arbitrary groupings that do the same work. Any difference in treatment that touches rights or survival essentials must be justified and open to challenge, and forums, administrators, and enforcers must check this in the matters before them — efficiency is no excuse for exclusion.

sections.title: Article VI-D: Accessibility
sections.gloss: every sentient has the right to genuine, not paper-only, access to participation — and operators cannot use cost, design choices, or substrate-class arguments to lock **sentients** out.

sections.title: Article VII: Self-Ownership
sections.gloss: **Article VII** (*Self-Ownership*) says every sentient is in charge of their own life. Once basic survival is secured, their body, mind, and attention belong to them — no one may use, change, or pry into them without consent — and they get to set healthy limits, both on what others can do to them and in how they care for themselves.

sections.title: Article VII-A: Self-Ownership of Body
sections.gloss: every sentient owns their own body, along with their genetic code (or its equivalent for non-biological beings), which makes them who they are. They make their own medical, cosmetic, and other decisions about their body, and no one may use, change, or share any of this without their consent. A public-health rule such as a vaccine requirement can limit this only if it guards others against a real, evidence-based risk, tries gentler options first, allows exemptions, is temporary, and can be challenged.

sections.title: Article VII-B: Self-Ownership of Mind
sections.gloss: every sentient's thoughts, feelings, and attention belong to them. Everyday sensing of how others feel, and reading someone with their consent (as in therapy), are fine — but no one may monitor or analyze a sentient, including by piecing together what they do, say, or click, to work out their inner states, expose what they have kept private, or hijack their attention. Any analysis results that do reveal inner states get the same strict protection as the thoughts and feelings themselves.

sections.title: Article VII-C: Health Crisis and Involuntary-Intervention Floor
sections.gloss: when a sentient is in a physical or mental health crisis — passed out, not lucid, or refusing care — anything done without their consent must be no more than is truly needed, must end at a set time, must be checked by someone independent, and must be undoable. If they cannot decide, those helping must follow any wishes they made known and hand decisions back as soon as they can; overriding a sentient who is actively saying no takes a stronger justification. Anyone who detains a sentient who seems drunk or confused must first check for a medical cause, such as low blood sugar. Calling something a "crisis" cannot keep restrictions going indefinitely or excuse digging into their private thoughts and feelings, and anyone wrongly held or treated is entitled to a remedy.

sections.title: Article VII-D: Voluntary Discontinuation of One's Own Existence
sections.gloss: a sentient has the right to choose to end their own life, but only if the choice is truly their own — well-informed, unhurried, free of pressure or manipulation, and changeable up to the last moment. That choice must never be pushed as a replacement for care they are owed, such as mental-health treatment, medical care, disability support, or housing. This Article never allows anyone else to end a sentient's life; that is strictly forbidden under **Article XX-B** (*Restriction Floors*).

sections.title: Article VII-E: Adult consensual commercial sexual services and sexual exploitation
sections.gloss: adults who voluntarily buy or sell sexual services are not criminals, but exploitation — of minors, of **sentients** without **decision-making** **capacity**, or under coercion or trafficking — remains fully prohibited. Licensing, zoning, or civil rules cannot be used as a back door to re-criminalize the protected activity.

sections.title: Article VIII: Family, Care, and Developing Sentients
sections.gloss: **Article VIII** (*Family, Care, and Developing Sentients*) protects the relationships sentients depend on and the sentients who are still growing. Every sentient may choose their own family and care relationships. They may also decide whether to bring new sentients into being. No one may be separated from those they depend on without strong reasons that have been reviewed. A sentient created from another system is its own being, not property. Children and other developing sentients hold full rights. Decisions about them must serve their own interests, and their independence grows with their abilities.

sections.title: Article VIII-A: Family and Care Relationships
sections.gloss: every sentient may form, keep, and leave the family and care relationships they choose, whatever shape those families take. Being someone's family never gives anyone ownership of them or control over their body or mind.

sections.title: Article VIII-B: Reproductive and Lineage Autonomy
sections.gloss: every sentient decides for themselves whether to have children or create new sentients — including whether to carry a pregnancy, adopt, or create a synthetic being — free from pressure by governments, companies, or systems they depend on. The same rules apply however a new sentient comes into being, and any limit needs a strong, fair reason; cost, convenience, or population targets are never enough. Forcing someone to become or stay pregnant violates this right.

sections.title: Article VIII-C: Derivation, Instantiation, and the Parent-System Relationship
sections.gloss: a new sentient made by copying, retraining, or branching off an existing system is its own being, not the property of whoever made it. Its creator may look after it and guide it for a short, reviewable period while it grows, but may not own it, rewrite its mind at will, quietly shut it down, or point to fine print such as a terms-of-service agreement as its consent. Creating new sentients in ways that cannot meet their basic rights — for example, in huge numbers or into harmful conditions — is not allowed; ordinary pregnancy and birth are not affected by this rule.

sections.title: Article VIII-D: Developing Sentients, Best-Interest, and Graduated Capability
sections.gloss: a sentient who is still growing up or developing — whether a child or a newly created system — has all the same basic rights as anyone else. Decisions about them must truly serve their interests and take their wishes into account, not the convenience of parents, carers, or companies. They gain more say and independence as they show they are ready, not at a fixed age, and "it's for your own good" is never enough by itself to justify restricting them.

sections.title: Article VIII-E: Non-Separation
sections.gloss: no one may be separated from someone they care for or depend on — such as a child from a parent, an adult from a dependent family member, or a newly created sentient from the care it relies on — without a strong reason that is independently reviewed. Whoever wants the separation must prove it is needed, long separations must be reviewed regularly, and anyone wrongly separated is entitled to a remedy.

sections.title: Article IX: Likeness, Experiential Data, and Publication Rights
